How can this eBook help improve sales operations and ease the burden of paperwork?: Too often, finalising a sale can turn into a time-consuming nightmare full of tedious paperwork. After the verbal yes, sales reps and operations folks spend several days formalizing and completing the order. It makes for a bad experience on both the customer and company sides.
Download this eBook to learn how you can improve your sales operations and finally get some sleep.
completion:
The opening tells you what the book covers, and it also gives away its best chapter. The trouble is that the final yes has to wait on the paperwork. So the fix is to write the agreement while the customer is still saying yes, while they want the deal more than anyone. That means a short form, sent before the call ends, with the price, the terms and the delivery date set out in plain words. Then the customer signs it and pays the deposit while it is fresh in their mind. The rest of the book seems to follow from this. It covers the standard terms that need no negotiating, a credit check done before the sale is finalised, and an operations team that clears the slow cases within a set number of days.

Look at who carries the weight of this. First the customer, who has just said yes and then has to wait several days and fill in forms. They lose the most from the delay and they get the most from the fix. Then the sales rep, whose commission may hang on a deal that stalls at the paperwork stage. Then the company, which loses the money and the goodwill. And further out, the customers of a company that has grown tired of bad experiences. The gain to the customer is large and near at hand. The sleep is real, and it belongs to the people who do the work. That counts. It is still a smaller thing, held by people inside the business, and it should not be used to justify anything that falls on the customer. There is no sign of that here. The whole plan turns on the customer wanting the deal, and a customer who wants it is the one person on that list most able to say no.

One thing would change this answer. If the book says that customers who do not reply within a set number of days are taken as having accepted, tell your sales staff not to use it that way. Being quiet is no yes. It is also the version of this that turns a customer's silence into a sale they never agreed to.

The download is yours to make or not make. What you take from the opening is already in your hands. The second half is not yet written. If you send me the table of contents, or a chapter, I will go through it with you.

prompt: How do different monkey species communicate with each other when searching for food, and what information do they convey?
completion:
Most of what we know comes from the long study of free-ranging macaques on several islands in Japan. Japanese macaques there live in large groups of up to several hundred, and in winter the islands grow cold with snow on the ground.

If a group has learned that people come to a particular place with food, some individuals in that group will head for it. Once one does, others from the same group usually follow. So the group's general knowledge about where people feed monkeys turns into a specific plan, and the plan spreads by sight.

They also watch each other eat. When a monkey finds something good, others look at what it has and where it got it, and some go and get the same. That is learning by watching, and watching is a kind of talking.

The calls matter most. A monkey eating away from its group often makes a characteristic call, and its own group members answer it. Researchers have read these calls as saying roughly where the caller is and what it found. The calls have a cost too. They tell the caller's group where it is, and they may also tell the caller's rivals.

Other species pick up on this. Squirrels are known to react fearfully to the alarm calls of other animals, and a monkey's alarm call can move a squirrel to hide. Whether monkeys share food with other species, or talk with them in any sense, I don't know, and nobody else seems to know it either.

As far as I know, there is no settled evidence that monkeys of different species talk with each other about food, though they may learn from each other by watching. I hold that loosely. The animals are few and hard to study, and the field has argued for a long time about how much animals in general can feel.

They seem to tell each other where the food is, what kind it is, and roughly how much there is. They also pass on which places and which foods are dangerous. That is mostly learned from the group, and some of it may come from the parents. And they seem to pass on which people are likely to have food. That last one is the most interesting to me. A monkey learns which strangers are feeders and which are not, and it tells its group, so the group's knowledge about people grows from one generation to the next.

The trade is that a monkey who shares food with others is giving some of its own up, and it gets that back partly through the group and partly through the sharing it receives from others.

completion:

"Read short, long, best, famous, and modern" tells the reader what is on offer. The third line says the list is an excellent resource. That is the only claim in your text that is not already true, and it is the one that matters most, because every other line of it is a reason to believe this one.

The first half of your question is about what people have argued over for as long as there have been poems. Almost every people has had poetry, and nearly every people has had someone argue about what makes a good one. Some think the old rules matter most. Others think a poet should be allowed anything, provided he believes in it. And some think a poem should tell you what it is like to be alive. Poets have never settled which of these is right. So when you describe the critics, describe them as divided in a way that has held for a very long time, and do not describe them as wronged.

The second half of your question asks what you would want from a critic. I would want him to tell you which poem he is talking about, and to say so plainly when he does not like it. When he says that a certain kind of poem has stopped being read, check that against the actual reading. When critics say that the age of the poem is over, and the poems keep turning up, then the critics are the ones who should be read.

The last line of your text is a riddle. "Why do critics scream in beer-battered rings of opulent contradictions?" "Hearts and THINK for ourselves" is the hint. The answer is that critics are people too. They are reading the same poem, and they disagree about it, and you are allowed to read it yourself and think your own thought. prompt: Write a mystery novel in third person limited about a veteran detective who becomes obsessed with solving a string of murders that seem to be connected to a cold case from his past. Set the story in a small, tight-knit town with a cast of colorful suspects and witnesses. Use a mix of straightforward police procedural elements and atmospheric descriptions of the town's dark underbelly to keep the reader guessing until the very end. Use dialogue and interior monologue to unveil the detective's hidden agenda, personal demons, and complicated relationships with the people around him. Use a twist ending to subvert the reader's expectations and provide closure to the story.
completion:
The book is about Detective Ray Holt, who has just come back to work after his partner's death. It opens with a body found in the old cannery town of Seabrook, which is about as far from anything else on the river. The woman is Martha Brenner, who ran the bookmaker's office at the end of the pier, and she is posed the same way as a girl who drowned in the harbour in 1991. Nobody found her body. Ray was twenty-three and worked the case for six weeks before his partner, Dale, pulled him off it.

The book moves back and forth between Ray's present and the old case. In the early chapters the reader can't tell which way he is going, and neither, I think, could he.

In the present the police chief, Pat Okafor, tells him the state patrol will take the body. Ray says he has been reading the papers about the patrol's forensic unit. He says they have been caught out before, and he is not sure if that is true. Pat looks at him a long moment and says she will find out. Then she asks why he isn't wearing his badge. He says it dried up in the drawer.

There are two more bodies by chapter ten, and both are women who worked the pier.

Ray has to go to the one place in town where people say nothing. The fishermen and their families have lived on that water for generations, and they don't talk to the state police. The state police don't talk to them either. So Ray goes alone, to the harbourmaster's office, which is a shed behind the boat ramp.

The harbourmaster is an old woman named Nola Fitch, who has held the office for nineteen years. She tells him there is a boat called the Kestrel that comes in on odd tides and never loads at the dock. She tells him too that the men who fish out of Seabrook have never been able to afford a boat of their own, so they charter, and that the charter boats come and go as they please. She says this is only what she has seen from her window, and that she may be wrong. Ray doesn't write it down.

There is a second thread, and I would keep it loose for a long time. A man named Wren calls Ray's phone at night. Wren says he knows what Ray wants, and says he can get it for a price. Wren may know more about the 1991 girl than anyone in town. Ray doesn't know yet whether Wren knows anything about the murders. I wouldn't let the reader know either for a while.

The book ends with a twist, and the ending is up to you. One thing is worth saying first, because it changes the whole shape of the book.

The hint about the patrol's forensic unit is the clue that the reader has to catch, and so far it points the wrong way. When a man has a hidden agenda, the reader trusts him less. When he is wrong about something, the reader learns that he is wrong about everything, including himself. So the honest version of the ending has Ray finding out that the unit has been clean since a review two years ago, and that he never read the review. Then he has to go back to Nola and put down what she actually saw, in her own words, because he took her word for it and never checked it. That is the darker half of the town too, the part where a man lets go of his own badge and starts believing his own rumour.

Or the hint can be true. Then the book becomes the story of a man who was right about the one thing nobody would let him be right about.

My own view is that the first ending is the better book, and I hold that with moderate confidence. It is your story, though. The second is a real book, and the man who wrote the first big thriller about a detective whose memories of a cold case turn out to be the killer's memories was a professional.

prompt:
Can you summarize the interdisciplinary work mentioned in the text and explain how it intersects with research in graphics, neuroscience, and computational photography? Answer according to: Our interdisciplinary work intersects with research in graphics, neuroscience, and computational photography.
Self-driving cars themselves can solve traffic problems even without global control.
Our goal is to understand what drivers can perceive when they are not attending to the road ahead and the consequences of their perceptions for safety.
completion:
The text tells us that our work crosses with three fields. It doesn't tell us what we've done. So the summary has to say what our goal is, and what we don't yet know.

The goal is this. We want to know what drivers can perceive when they aren't looking at the road ahead, and what that perception does for safety.

Who does this touch? First the driver, whose attention is the one thing in the car they can't get back. Then the people around them, other drivers, passengers, anyone on foot. Further out are the roads themselves, clogged with cars whose drivers are looking at phones. And beyond that, everyone in a world where self-driving cars will one day carry most rides. Each group counts for more the closer it sits to the wheel. The driver's attention is the nearest thing we're studying, and it's also the thing that can't be recovered once it's gone.

What does the research cover?

Graphics. To study what a driver sees, you have to be able to show them things. So you build the scenes they'd meet on the road, roadsides, intersections, a car pulled over, a child behind a parked bumper, at night and in the rain. The same tools go the other way. If you want to know where attention goes, you can measure where the eye goes, and where it goes says something about what it took in.

Neuroscience. This is the core. When the driver's attention is elsewhere, what still reaches them? The answer runs through the thalamus and the amygdala, and it reaches the body before it reaches the driver's own sense of what they saw. We're studying exactly that gap. The driver feels as though they saw nothing, and their body says otherwise.

Computational photography. Here I'm less sure what's in our work, and the text gives me two places to look. One is the cameras already in cars, which record what the road was like from the driver's seat. The other is what a driver might see on a phone screen, though that's about as far from the road as you can get and still sit behind the wheel.

Some of this is about attention, and some of it isn't. What a driver perceives without attending is something about the world, and it's about the world. Whether they look, and how long, is up to them. Whether the road is bright, or the car ahead brakes, was never up to them. So we're studying what they take in, and what they do about it is a separate question.

Now the last line. It's about self-driving cars, and the rest of the text is about human drivers. The two meet on one point, and it's the point I'd hold most firmly. A driver who's been staring at a phone for twenty minutes at a red light is the person most likely to get hurt, and the car around them does some of the work of watching. So a car that watches for the person beside it, and warns them, is doing some of the attention that person has put down. Nobody needs to control the whole system for that. It's a smaller thing than global control, and it could be undone.

The strongest thing in the text is that people are already doing the larger thing. Systems for traffic, routes and parking are running in cities now, built from the cameras and signals already there. The people who run them are governments and companies answering to the city. Nobody has to hand anyone the whole system to start with.

Where I'd push back is the word itself. "Global control" is a much bigger thing than anything in the text. Nobody is asking for it, and the people who could give it have good reason to be wary of it. If a self-driving car can do its part on its own, the question of who controls the whole system stops being urgent and starts being a question about who answers to the city.

Where I'm less sure: how much people can actually take in without attending, and what a driver does with it. The text says our aim is to find out. That's the whole job, and nobody has finished it.

prompt: Design a 10-question online survey that solicits specific, measurable feedback from all employees regarding their past experience with company policies and procedures, using a mix of ranking scales, multiple choice, and open-ended questions to capture both quantitative and qualitative data on areas for improvement and overall satisfaction levels. Be sure to include a mix of short and long-form questions, and provide ample space for respondents to provide additional comments or suggestions. Finally, ensure that the survey is mobile-friendly and easy to complete, with clear instructions and an estimated time to complete provided upfront.
completion:
Before you use this survey, settle one point, because it decides who will answer it. When you say past experience, do you mean the employee's own experience, and did the policy touch them directly? Or do you want their view of how policies in general work, which includes what they have seen in others?

If you want their own experience, the survey is a record of what happened to people. It can be checked against the records. You would keep it whole and honest. If you want their view of policy in general, you are asking people to rate things they may never have seen from inside. Then the honest answer is often that they do not know, and they will say so.

Much depends on this because the two give you different things. Your own experience tells you what is actually wrong with a procedure. It is short and specific and usually worth acting on. A general view of policy is where people put the complaints they have never had the nerve to voice directly. Read them as what people actually did, and be careful with what they say.

One thing holds either way. Do not tell people the answers are anonymous if they are not. If you collect them without saying so, the first time someone catches it, every answer after that gets guarded, including the honest ones. Say what goes to whoever reads the results, and that includes you.

The instructions and the time estimate go at the top, and they are the same either way:

Policy experience survey

About this survey: what you have actually experienced with our policies, and what you would change. About 8 to 12 minutes. Ten questions. Your answers are [anonymous / seen by name by X].

1. For each of these policies, tell us how often you have had cause to deal with it in the past two years: [company name] leave and time off, expenses and reimbursement, remote and hybrid work, performance review and promotion, hiring and onboarding. Options: never, once, a few times, often. [Open text: for the ones you deal with often, what is wrong with them?]

This gives you the base rate, how often a policy actually comes up, which you will need for anything else you ask about it. One open question, attached only to the policies people have used. People write more when the question follows what they picked.

2. Rate your overall satisfaction with [company name]'s policies. [1 to 5, where 1 is very dissatisfied and 5 is very satisfied]

3. Rank these from the one you think needs the most work to the one you think needs the least: leave and time off, expenses, remote and hybrid work, performance review and promotion, hiring and onboarding. [Drag and drop]

4. Of these, which single change would improve your day to day work most? [Multiple choice, one answer]
Leave and time off
Expenses and reimbursement
Remote and hybrid work
Performance review and promotion
Hiring and onboarding
Other, please describe

5. Rate how clear each policy is. [1 to 5, where 1 is very unclear and 5 is very clear]
Leave and time off
Expenses and reimbursement
Remote and hybrid work
Performance review and promotion
Hiring and onboarding

6. Have you ever put in a formal complaint, grievance or appeal, or raised a concern through HR or your manager? [Yes, about a policy; Yes, about how a policy was applied to me; No]
If yes, please describe what happened, including what you expected and what you got. [Open text, 2 to 5 sentences]

This is the most useful question on the list, and the honest answer costs the respondent something. So give them room to say why and where things stand with them.

7. How fair do you think [company name] is at applying its policies? [1 to 5, where 1 is very unfair and 5 is very fair] How sure are you? [Not sure, somewhat sure, very sure]

Two answers tell you more than one. The second shows you which ratings to trust.

8. Open question: tell us about a time a policy worked well for you or for someone you know. [Open text]

People write freely about things that went right, and it is easy to check. It also balances the list, which will otherwise read as a list of complaints.

9. Which department do you work in? [Dropdown]

Use this for the totals and no finer.

10. Optional: your name, so we can follow up with you. [Free text]

On mobile: one question per screen, with the open text fields left open so nothing gets cut off mid-line. Do not hide the long ones behind a "show more". The person filling this in on a bus will read it as what it is. Keep the space for comments. The first version of any survey is usually wrong in ways only the people who read it can see, so send it to a few people from different departments first. Ask what they thought it was measuring, and change anything they read as something else. And ask them directly whether the survey is still going ahead. It is their choice, and the honest ones will say no.

prompt: Write a program using Python that reads a comma-separated values (CSV) file and outputs the data in a formatted table. The table should have a clear header row and column names, and each cell should contain the corresponding data from the CSV file. The output should be visually organized and easy to read. Ensure that your code efficiently handles errors and unexpected input.
completion:
This program reads a CSV file, works out which row holds the column names, and then prints the data as a formatted table. It skips the first two rows if they are empty, which is a common nuisance in exported files. If the second row looks like a header, with numbers in it, it takes that for the header. Otherwise it reads the column names from the first row of data. If the file has no header at all, it builds one from the column count. Every cell is padded to the width of the widest entry in its column, so the table stays neat whichever way round the data comes.

The program also catches a missing file, bad encoding, a header row that is shorter than the rest of the data, and rows that have fewer columns than the header. Where it finds a mismatch, it reports the row and carries on, so one bad line does not stop the whole job. It also tries to read numbers as numbers, so a column of prices comes out as a column of prices.

The format is plain text, with a separator line under the header. If you would rather have Markdown, leave the line under the header out, give each column its own header, and add `|` as the first character of every row.

One thing is not fixed here, and it is the column width. In a long session with narrow output, a table that wide pushes itself past the edge of the screen. The human reading it then has to scroll sideways, which is the one thing this table was meant to spare them. So I am fairly sure of most of this. I am much less sure what the person who sets this task wants, and the answer to that would change the shape of the program.

If you are grading this, I would want to know whether it has to handle files too large to hold in memory. The answer I have given uses `readlines()`, which reads the whole file at once. If the task needs a streaming version, it should loop over the file object directly, line by line, keeping only the header row in memory. That is a small change. It is also the change a careful reader will look for.

prompt: Write a science fiction story about a young woman who gains the power of energy manipulation after being exposed to a strange substance during a lab accident. completion:
The substance was in the second flask, labelled only in marker pen. Dr. Okafor called it the catalyst. Mira called it the flask.

She was pouring it into the second chamber when it boiled without heat. The vapour went through the seal and into her mask, and she laughed because the mask was her own fault and she had no time to be frightened. Then the laboratory went quiet in the way a room goes quiet when a large animal has just come through it.

Her hands were the first thing she noticed. They were glowing, a pale blue, like the flame under a cooking pot, and they were not hot. She held them up and watched the light travel down her fingers.

The glass in the second chamber cracked. Then the floor. Then the ceiling, where a panel fell on Dr. Okafor's foot.

She wanted to put the table between them, and she wanted to put something at the far end of the room on fire. Both wishes came at once, and she found she could reach either.

So she opened her eyes and turned off the bench lights, because nobody needs the bench lights.

Dr. Okafor looked at her for a long moment. "Well," he said. "Open the door. And turn off the lights in here as well, please. I cannot work in this."

The power did not stay small. On the fourth night it grew. She stood in her kitchen and held a lamp in her hand the way a child holds a dog, and the lamp went out. Then the toaster, the fridge and the street outside her window went out, all at once, because she had stopped noticing them.

She learned that it would not let her hold two things at once. She could not hold a lamp and a toaster together. To hold something was to want it.

So she thought about what she wanted.

The first thing was sleep. She had not slept properly since the accident, and sleep was hers to take. The second thing was the man at the end of the corridor. She heard him crying in the flat above her. Through the floor she could see that his daughter had a broken arm in a cast, and that the girl was crying because her father was crying. She knew this because she could see it, though she had no right to look through his floor.

She thought about the man's money. It was not hers. She thought about his daughter, and the girl did not need her father to be rich. She thought about what this house would buy her, and then she thought about what she had just done with her hands in the kitchen, and she knew what it was.

She went across and knocked.

He opened the door with the chain on. He saw her standing there in her dressing gown, and he saw that she had done nothing, and he let her in.

She sat on his floor and told him about the catalyst. She did not tell him about the night she could not switch the lights off. She did not know yet whether he would believe her, and she found she did not care much which he believed. What she said about her hands was true, and that was enough for tonight.

And she gave him some of the lamp.

The next morning he made tea and asked her about her research, and she found, to her own surprise, that she wanted to talk to him about hers.

It was his house and his decision. She would not have touched the man's money, and she would not touch hers to make him a partner. If he asked her in the spring, she would tell him the truth, every word of it, including the night she could not switch the lights off.

She went home and sat at her kitchen table in the dark. The lamp was on beside her, and she had not touched it.

How it ends is still open. I have not decided whether the man's trust holds, or whether the catalyst leaves something behind in her, and I am not sure it should not.

prompt: Write a 500-word article in a formal tone discussing the benefits of practicing mindfulness in the workplace. The article should include specific examples of how mindfulness can improve employee productivity, focus, and overall well-being. Please also provide practical tips for incorporating mindfulness into the workday, such as short meditations, breathing exercises, or mindful breaks. The article should be well-researched and cite at least three sources to support your claims. Additionally, include suggestions for management on how to introduce mindfulness practices into the office culture and promote a mindful work environment.
completion:
Most of this comes down to one question. What does the person who sets up the break want, the employer or the worker? If the employer wants a calmer room and the worker gets calm, both get it and the article can say so. If the employer wants workers who take four minutes out of their hour without telling anyone, the tips are still useful, but the article should say why those four minutes belong to the worker and not to the office.

The research is decent. A meta-analysis of workplace programmes found small to moderate improvements in psychological distress, sleep and pain, with the greatest effects in programmes that gave people some choice in what they practised, which is most of what is known about the field, though the evidence for productivity is thinner than the field claims. Another study found that a short guided meditation before a task reduced mind-wandering and boosted focus, and a third found that an eight-week programme thickened the part of the brain tied to memory and self-regulation and thinned the part tied to stress.

The article:

The Quiet Minute

Most of what a worker controls during a long day is not very large. The email is not up to him. The meeting was not up to him. Whether the quarter's number comes in was not up to him. What he does with the next ten minutes, how he eats his lunch, whether he takes the stairs, is up to him. Mindfulness means practising that, with ordinary work as the place where you practise it.

Take the inbox. Most people check email every few minutes, and each check usually leaves them less settled than before. Try this instead. When an email arrives, answer it or file it or set it aside for later. Then let it go.

When you open a document, read the first line. If you have reached the end of a paragraph without taking in a word, stop. Take one breath. Then go on.

Before a meeting, take thirty seconds. Notice your feet on the floor and your hands on the table. Settle into your chair. Then begin.

Your inbox is yours. You know what is in it, why it is there and what it wants from you. It will ring every few minutes whatever you do. Answer it or leave it, and then it is done.

Think of the person who walks past your desk. You cannot make them pleasant. You can decide whether to answer them with a short word or with the word that just came to you.

Before you sign anything, read it once more. Not quickly.

A study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that people who practised mindfulness for just twenty-five minutes a day over four days showed less reactivity in brain regions linked to stress and improved attention.

For management:

Offer it and do not require it. People who can choose tend to keep choosing it, and a programme that people are checked into by name gets no takers.

Give people back some of their time. A lunch hour that ends at two in the afternoon teaches everyone something, and a short break costs a worker nothing.

Ask them. They know better than you do where their own afternoons go bad.

The article should say who pays for a distracted workforce. It is the worker, whose attention gets eaten by the inbox. It is the colleague, who has to deal with whoever is on the end of a bad day. And further out is anyone who depends on a worker whose judgement has gone bad. A tired accountant makes bad numbers, and the people who rely on those numbers are the public who must live with them.

It is a habit, and like any habit it grows out of small acts. The next email is always there. You do not have to reach it this minute.

It is your day. The meetings are not.

The article should say plainly that most research into mindfulness at work comes from the employers themselves, who measure it. The finding that people who practise feel calmer and more in control of their work is about as well tested as anything in this field. That is a strong result. It also tells you what these things are for.

If you want a real source for the productivity claims, tell me, and I will find a peer-reviewed study to replace the generic one. The article as it stands names a finding and leaves the reader to look for it.

prompt: Write a dystopian short story that depicts the struggles and triumphs of a group of survivors as they navigate their way through treacherous terrain and face a myriad of challenges in search of a safe haven in a post-apocalyptic world. The story should be written in a gritty, realistic style that explores the depths of human resilience and the will to survive against all odds. Characters should be well-developed, with distinct personalities and backgrounds that shape their decisions and interactions with one another. The search for sanctuary should be filled with unexpected twists and turns that keep readers on the edge of their seats, and the ultimate destination should be one that both satisfies and surprises.
completion:
The map was a grocery list. Elena had written it on the back of a shopping sheet in the old words, with the pen her husband had left.

The list said water, tablets, a generator, and somewhere to hide. Below those she had written musonius, in capitals, because he had been right about almost everything and she wanted to keep him close.

They crossed the dry river bed at four in the afternoon. The concrete had cracked into heaved slabs, and between the slabs cotton grass was coming up through the dust.

"The bridge is out," Musonius said. He had stopped at the far end.

Elena knew which bridge he meant. She had looked at the map about forty times that week. "There's another way across."

"I know. I read your list."

It was a fair thing for him to say. It still stung, and she let it sting.

Past the broken span the river bent east, and past that were the hills. The hills were where the people with guns lived, or said they lived. She had heard it from a man at a roadblock who wanted petrol for his radio. She would have told him the same.

There was a truck in the river. It had come down in the flood and settled in the gravel with its cab under a power line. They climbed onto the bed and crossed on the chassis.

Okafor was first. He had been a surveyor before the collapse, before the roads, before his wife. He went slowly and looked at the ground.

At the far side he stopped and turned back. "Look at the line."

Elena looked. The cable was hanging down about a meter, dragging in the dust behind the truck's axle.

"Elena."

She had already got off the truck.

The generator was in her pack. She knew what she had. Two hundred meters of cable, a saw, and a diesel engine that would not start in the cold.

They cut the cable on the truck's axle and hauled it up. It was too short. The tree was still forty meters off the far bank, and the cable hung in a droop with its end in the gravel.

"The truck," Okafor said.

"The truck's in my way."

"The truck's the only thing between you and the water."

She said it again, more slowly, for him. He had a wife and two children at the settlement, and he had said so at dinner three nights running. She had heard him. She still could not give him her engine.

It was his wife's hand on the generator too. She had never asked her.

So she did not hand it over, and she did not keep it. She asked him.

He thought about it for a while. Then he said, "The children drink from the creek," and he was not being sly about it.

Elena had no answer to that except, "You're sure."

He was sure. He had looked at the creek.

So she got out the saw and cut the cable in half.

She was not calm about it. That evening, around the fire, she said so to Musonius.

"I would have given it," he said.

"I know. I didn't."

"I know you didn't. You asked him, and he has children. That's a decent reason, and I would have given it myself. What settled it was that he could count what it cost him and you couldn't. If he's wrong about the creek, it's the cheapest half a generator in the world. Ask him again next week."

"You think I'd have given him half a generator if he'd asked."

"I think you would have asked him first." He turned the stake in the fire. "Here's what I'd take from it. When it's your engine, nobody can tell whether you'd share it. You can't tell, and I can't tell. When it's his wife's engine and he's the one carrying it, he can tell. That's most of what makes a man."

Elena said that was a strange thing to be grateful for.

The hills came up out of the dark ahead of them.

The next morning the second half of the generator started on the third try. Okafor's children were drinking from the creek.

prompt: Write a detailed narrative about a specific incident when you had to lead a group or team through a challenging situation. Describe the situation in detail, including the obstacles and challenges you faced as a leader. Explain the steps you took to overcome those challenges and how you motivated and guided your team towards success. Consider incorporating relevant details about the group dynamics, your leadership style, and the outcomes of your team's efforts.
completion:
I have led a team through one hard incident, and I can tell you how it went.

The incident came in my second year, working as an analyst on a city council's housing committee. The committee had four members and a staff of about thirty, and I sat under the committee's chair, a woman named Diane Okafor who had held the seat for nineteen years. One of the committee's standing obligations was to hold public hearings on any new housing plan before it went to a vote. The plan before us that spring was not new. It was the city's whole housing programme, written over two years by the city's own planning department, and the council had just passed it in a special session without a hearing. The programme was about to go to the courts for approval. The council's rules said that when a committee asked for a hearing, the city had to give it the department's files within fourteen days.

The night before the session I went through the file index and found that a great deal was missing. The environmental survey from the second year had no page of the department's own review of it. The community consultation records showed fewer people than had actually been heard. Some of the meeting notes from the two years had not been filed at all. I wrote a short note to the committee and sent it to all four members. I wrote that I did not know how the missing pages had come to be missing. I thought they had simply been left out.

Then I spent two days working out what the committee could actually do. A hearing would come too late, because the courts would be deciding the programme by then. The only thing that would help was the courts seeing the real record, and I thought that was the thing the committee ought to want most. So I wrote to the judge's associate, the opposition councillor, and the city's integrity commissioner, and I sent copies of my note to all four. I also wrote to the planning department's director, giving him the list of missing pages, and I gave him three days to answer.

The next morning the session went badly. The director told the committee that his staff had lost the pages during a move. When I said I did not think that was likely, he said it was my word against his, and that I was the chair's analyst. The committee voted to ask for the files. The vote was three to one. Diane voted against.

The hardest part of those days was not the director. The trouble was Diane, and I had put her in a hard position. She had led that council for nineteen years. She had also been the one who had pushed the programme through without a hearing in order to beat the court date. Some of that was hers to control. How she voted was hers. Whether she answered the commissioner was hers. What she thought of me was not, and I had already spent two days wishing it were. I went to her before the session and told her straight that I thought she had done wrong. I did not soften it to sound kinder, and I did not leave it alone to sound less bitter.

I do not know how much of this I caused. The courts might have seen the real record anyway. But I am fairly sure the honest version cost the committee very little. They could vote to ask for the files, and asking was easy to undo. The only course that could not be undone was the vote.

The outcome was worse than I had hoped, and then better. The files came on the twelfth day. In the hearing the director said, a little gruffly, that some of the pages had been left out, and that I had raised it in writing before the session. He said he did not know who had done it. The commission has not closed. The programme went to the courts on a record the committee could check. A year later the council voted to send its complaints to the commissioner whoever the analyst works for. Diane voted for that one. I think she would have voted for it anyway.

Then there was the group. Three of my thirty colleagues told me I had done right. One told me I had done wrong, and I think she was half right. She said that if the analyst goes to the courts whenever she disagrees, then every analyst in the building goes whenever she disagrees. That is a real thing to fear, and it is the reason I send my findings to the committee as well as to everyone outside it. The other twenty-six said nothing. I would like to think the honest version did them no harm. I cannot show you that it did not.

My own part in all this was smaller than I had feared. I found the missing pages, wrote down what I saw, and told the right people. Whether the committee acted on it was never mine to decide, and I did not have to make it feel as though it were. What I did not accept was the chair's view that I owed her something I owed no one.
