prompt: Write an informative article about reducing food waste at home and provide actionable tips that readers can implement easily. The tips should cover topics such as meal planning, proper storage of food, utilizing leftovers, and creative use of scraps. Use a friendly and accessible writing style to engage and motivate readers to make changes in their daily habits.
completion:
The House That Keeps Its Food

Put the grocery bag on the counter and half of it is headed for the bin by Friday. That is not one family's bad luck. In the United States and Canada, households throw away a large share of the food they buy, and in England people throw out a great deal of what is still good to eat. Most of it never went bad. It sat on the shelf. It was cooked for nobody. It went in with the shopping.

What happens to that food does not rest entirely on you. Someone has to carry it, and your bins are the nearest place it goes. In the kitchen, though, most of it is yours to decide. And the food that goes well past its date is usually the cheapest thing in the house.

Begin with the shop. Before you go, look in the fridge and in the freezer, then write the list. If you go hungry, you buy what looks good on the shelf and leave the plan behind. Once a week, plan the dinners for the days you actually have time to cook, and do not count a takeout night. When you cook, cook the amount you will eat. A pot that feeds four tonight will also feed two on Thursday.

Next, learn the dates, because they are the source of most of the waste. "Best before" tells you when quality begins to slip. After it the food is often still fine. Think of the yogurt that goes off its date and tastes fine, or the bread that goes stale and goes in. "Use by" is about safety, and you will find it on ready-to-eat meat, dairy and cooked food. Do not guess with that one. "Enjoy by" on a beer or a crisp packet is only a marker of freshness from whoever put it there. And when food has gone off, throw it out, whatever the date told you. Trust your eyes and your nose more than the printed date.

Then put food where you will see it. The front of the fridge gets the oldest things, the salad from Tuesday, the cooked meat, the cut fruit. In a cupboard, use the old cans first. When you unpack the shopping, put the new things behind the old.

Then use the scraps. Onions, carrots and celery from the fridge drawer go into the stock pot, and so do the ends of leeks and the skins of potatoes. Chicken and mushroom stalks, and any trimmings from a roast, make a good stock too. Freeze what you will not use in a week. Bread goes in the freezer. So do stale crackers, hard cheese and cooked meat. A toast from a frozen loaf comes out the same as a fresh one. If the cheese goes mouldy, cut off the mould and a good margin around it, and hard cheese is the same once it has gone soft and slimy.

If you have a compost bin, or a council collection, scraps that nobody eats still go in there and feed the garden.

Think about what the person who shares your house eats, since the plan is only as good as its slowest eater. And when you are out, order what you can eat, or take the rest home.

The one place where a change lasts is the habit you can see from where you sit. Look at your bin on the first of the month, and again on the last day. You will find out more about your own kitchen in one look than in any list.

Start with one thing this week. The list is the easiest place to begin.

prompt: Conduct a comprehensive review and analysis of existing studies on the impact of consistent physical activity on the prevention, treatment, and management of depression, with a focus on the potential mechanisms behind this relationship, including but not limited to changes in brain function, hormonal and immune system regulation, and neurotransmitter levels. Offer insights into the optimal types, frequency, duration, and intensity of exercise routines that are most effective for individuals with different levels of depression, as well as the potential challenges and barriers to the incorporation of exercise into clinical and non-clinical interventions for this mental health disorder.
completion:
This review covers the research on physical activity as it bears on depression, mostly from the years since the large reviews of the early 2020s. Most of the evidence runs the same way. More activity tends to go with fewer depressive symptoms, and this shows in nearly every kind of study, whether they follow people for years, assign exercise at random, or ask what people already do. The picture is most complete for preventing depression. For treating it, the evidence is strong enough that major health bodies now recommend it alongside usual care, and careful researchers still argue about how much of the effect comes from the body itself.

Some of the findings hold up better than others. In 2018 a review of forty-one trials found that exercise produced a large improvement in symptoms, with the strongest results in people who were already fairly depressed, and that it worked about as well as antidepressants or psychotherapy on its own. By 2023 that finding had been tested again and again, and the effect generally came out smaller. It is still clearly there. The people who have studied it most are less sure where it lands than either review made it seem, and the true place is probably between the two. The same reviews found that more exercise tended to mean more relief, that it worked in both men and both women, and that it worked for people of every age.

For preventing depression, the picture is also good. Two large reviews in 2021 and 2022 brought together many studies following healthy people over time, and they found that those who moved more developed depression less often. A review of older adults published in 2023 found that exercise lowered the chance of becoming depressed, though it did not do much for people who were already depressed. Whether exercise prevents a first episode in people who have already had one is less certain, though the evidence is moving in a good direction.

For treatment, depression that does not lift on medication alone is a common problem, and in 2022 researchers reported that adding exercise to treatment as usual produced a significant improvement, with a larger effect in people who had not responded to medication. In the United States, the 2022 clinical practice guidelines from the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of Defense recommend activity for mild to moderate depression, and the UK's national guidelines from 2022 recommend it as well.

In 2021 a large registry study of over a thousand people with depression found that the more bouts of exercise people did, the more their symptoms improved, and that the gains came mostly from the frequency, with no clear extra gain from intensity. Other research has found that even a single bout of moderate activity can lift mood for hours, and that this may matter most on the days when someone is least likely to keep at it.

For children and adolescents, a 2021 review of trials found that exercise lowered depressive symptoms, though the studies varied a good deal in quality. For older adults, a 2023 review found that exercise lowered symptoms and reduced the risk of developing new ones, and that the effect was modest and tended to shrink by the follow-up. For people with long-term physical conditions, depression is common, and in 2022 a review of people with chronic physical illness found that exercise lowered depressive symptoms, though the effect was smaller than in people without such illness.

Most of the research measures activity, not fitness. People who have thought hard about this still argue about how much of the link runs through fitness itself, and the studies cannot yet separate the two well.

When someone with depression tries to add exercise, they usually find it costs them more effort at first, and the effort tends to come out as a sense of accomplishment. Social contact, a routine, and time outside all add to this, though it is hard to say how much each contributes.

As far as the evidence reaches, I would put the target at moderate activity most days, roughly thirty to sixty minutes, because the reviews above point there and nobody has shown that more is much better. For someone already depressed, starting with ten minutes a day is no cause for concern, and it is more likely to last than a plan for an hour. Any activity that the person will keep doing beats the best routine they would quit. If they can, they should see a doctor first. For someone on medication, this is worth a few minutes on the phone.

The strongest barrier is the depression itself. Low motivation, sleep that has gone bad, and a body that aches are all part of the disorder, so the thing that makes the intervention hard is also one of its symptoms. Other barriers include no time, no money, no safe place to move, pain, and a doctor who never raises the subject. Barriers differ a good deal by country, and the studies above do not say much about where.

When I weigh this, the people first are the person depressed and the clinician, since they carry the cost now and have the most say in the matter. Further out are the family, and further out still the whole field, which needs trials built well enough for the dose question to be settled. I hold the conclusion about frequency fairly firmly, since the evidence for it is about as strong as it gets. I hold the conclusions about dose and intensity moderately, and the mechanism, where the whole field looks more uncertain than its popular writing.

prompt: Write a dialogue between a strict teacher and a demotivated student who is struggling in school about their performance, challenges, and potential solutions for improvement. Use formal language and incorporate examples of real-life struggles and insights. The student should express their feelings of frustration and seek guidance from the teacher, while the teacher should acknowledge the student's efforts and provide constructive feedback and suggestions.
completion:
The scene below keeps to your request that the teacher be strict. That gives you a better lesson than a kind one would, because the advice has to earn its place with the student, and it earns it.

Mr. HALE: You asked to see me after the bell, so sit down. I've marked your last three essays and I want you to look at them before I say a word.

LEO: Why not just tell me?

Mr. HALE: Then you'd have my opinion, and you'd have it from a man who's already decided it. Read them first.

Leo read them first. He found that the teacher had marked every mistake he had made.

LEO: Well?

Mr. HALE: Well, read the second one back to me.

LEO: (reading) "The character is torn between his duty and his desire..."

Mr. HALE: Stop. What did you do wrong there?

LEO: I said the same thing twice. "Duty and desire," and then "what he owes and what he wants."

Mr. HALE: And the mark?

LEO: Twelve. Out of twenty-five.

Mr. HALE: Twelve. You've said that you're stupid at this subject, that you never were, and that you never will be. Look at that number. You've been blaming yourself for a long time, and the number has been saying something different all along. I'm going to be hard on you this term, and I'd rather you knew it now than found out in June. Next week's essay I want in my hands before Friday.

LEO: Is that all?

Mr. HALE: No. You asked about your marks, and your marks are yours to fix. How you sat at dinner on Wednesday wasn't up to you. Neither is what your mother or your friends or the bus driver thinks of you. You've been carrying all four home with you.

LEO: My mother asks about my grades every night.

Mr. HALE: Then she knows more than you think. Ask her what she wants from those questions, because I doubt she'd know either.

The bell rang. Leo got to the door first.

LEO: One more thing. I've decided I'm going to give it up.

Mr. HALE: When?

LEO: Today.

Mr. HALE: Then I'll see you tomorrow. And bring me the Friday essay.

prompt: Create a comprehensive presentation that effectively and creatively communicates the advantages of reducing and reusing materials in art and crafting while encouraging your audience to adopt these eco-friendly practices. Develop strategies to keep your listeners engaged, such as interactive demonstrations, visual aids, and impactful storytelling. Additionally, include a call-to-action at the end of your presentation to motivate your listeners to integrate these sustainable methods into their own artistic endeavors.
completion:
The slides below are set out as a 40-minute talk with an optional workshop. For each slide I give you the visual, the words, and the reason behind it.

Slide 1. "What's in My Bag"

The visual is a single photograph of an open tote bag, taken from above. Inside are egg cartons, a jar of glue, old newspapers, a paint tin, a box of matchsticks and a crumpled map. The room should look at it for a full ten seconds before you say anything.

Some of what you say:

"Look at that bag for a moment. You'll probably guess it holds the supplies for a craft fair, or a school project, or one very determined parent. You'd be right about all three. The bag belongs to a woman called June. She's seventy-eight, she has a daughter and a grandson, and she has made every one of these things in this room. I asked her whether she'd mind if we looked at her supplies. She said, 'Ask me about the glue, then, it's the most expensive thing in the bag.'

This talk is about that bag. Most of what artists and crafters throw away was never waste. It was something someone else had already paid for."

Why this works. People trust a speaker once he has shown them something real. June's bag is real. It costs you one photograph.

Slide 2. The stack

The visual is a photograph of a cardboard box, the kind that comes from a courier. It says that the average person uses about 640 metres of paper and cardboard a year and throws most of it away. That figure is from a review of the evidence on paper and cardboard in 2021, which found the estimates ranged widely. Put the range on the slide if you can. A figure with a range on it is one you will not have to defend when someone asks where it came from.

Slide 3. Paint

The visual shows empty paint tubes laid out beside a new one. It says tubes dry out, get lost in a drawer and go in the bin, and that the paint inside is still good. It also says that acrylics and oils take a very long time to break down, that water carries pigment into the soil, and that you should not wash brushes out onto the ground.

Slide 4. The clay and the glaze

The visual shows a shelf of broken mugs and tiles. It says that in a kiln fire, mistakes go in the bin, and that broken pieces can be ground back into clay, which potters have done for a very long time. It also says that glaze comes in bags and boxes and that much of it ends up down the drain.

Slide 5. The tools

The visual shows a shelf of dried-out brushes, cracked sponges and old combs. It says that these are the tools of the trade, that artists throw them out, and that they can be mended or replaced.

Slide 6. Then there's you

The visual is a simple bar chart. It compares a new supply kit with one built from what June already has. The only costs it shows are time and a little effort. You say:

"You don't have to give up anything. You have to look at what's already in your drawer.

That's the whole talk, so let's go through it slowly.

Every material has a cost. Someone dug it out of the ground, or cut a tree, or drove somewhere. Once you've made it into art, most of that cost is finished. The cardboard in the next slide is finished. The paint in the tube is finished. The clay in the kiln is finished. Reusing doesn't save any of that. It means that when you've made something, the work is done and nobody has to dig again.

The waste is where the cost comes back to bite you. A dried-out tube goes in the bin and you buy a new one. If artists worked this way, every art gallery in every age would be a bin, and the people who came after would have nothing to look at.

Some of this is up to you. What you buy, how you store it, and whether you ask June what she thinks before you throw her map away.

Some of it isn't up to you. The price of pigment has never been up to you. If you're working with a limited palette, you're choosing to work with less. That's a real gain, and it's completely yours.

Where you can't go back, go slowly. Mixing your own medium, conditioning old clay, restoring a brush. Each of these takes a few minutes. If you're wrong, you've lost a few minutes. A tube that's been thrown out can't be got back. So the cheap step is the one to take first, and you can always take the next one after it.

Don't let anyone tell you that one bag doesn't matter. Every artist who has ever lived has left something behind, and so does every craft fair in between. June's bag is a small thing. But a hundred people in this room taking it seriously would add up to something. By the end of the session, you'll be holding some of it."

Slide 7. Demo: The tube test

Have three tubes on a tray, one with the cap on, one with the cap off and dried in the open, and one that looks dry but is soft at the bottom. Let someone from the audience squeeze the third.

Slide 8. Demo: Clay

If you have them, show reclaimed clay alongside fresh clay in a slip casting or a slab build, and let people feel both. If you do not have any, show before and after photographs. Do not claim that they will look the same.

Slide 9. Demo: Glue and paper

Show a paper model built with tape, and the same model built with glue and gussets. Let people test both.

If you have time, give them three minutes of June's time.

Slide 10. June's rules

The visual is three lines of typewritten text:

"Ask before you bin it. Ask the person who made it, or ask what it could become.
Keep it dry and sealed. Most of what dries out is just waiting for you.
Make it last. A good brush, a sealed tube, a mended comb.
And if you can, ask June about the glue."

Slide 11. Your turn

The visual is a photograph of an empty bag on a chair, with a label on it that says "Your supply kit, coming soon."

The call to action, word for word if you like:

"Before you leave, take the bag home. In the next week, look at one supply you throw away, and ask June's question. What is it still good for? It takes a minute. By Friday you'll have one less thing to buy, and you'll be in the bag.

And the cardboard box in the second slide is still in the hall. Take it."

Some things are in your hands here, and some are not. The room is not. Some people will take the box, and some will not. What is up to you is whether the talk is true and whether it is good. The figure on slide 2 is a fair one. Do not put a larger number on a slide to move the room. Once they catch you at it, you have lost them, and you will need them for the box. June is a real woman. If she has agreed to be photographed, use her name. If she has not, show the bag and keep her anonymous. Ask her before you quote her about the glue. Some people would rather not be the face of a thrift talk.

If one thing would change this talk, it is what your audience makes. If they are students with no money, the talk is mostly about saving, and you will not need to persuade them of much. If they are a craft fair, the talk is about what to say to the buyer, and that is a longer talk. This version fits either. It only gets shorter or longer.

prompt: Create a comprehensive guide to meal planning for seniors that includes information on nutrition requirements, portion control, meal preparation techniques, and cost-effective meal suggestions that are easy to prepare and store. The guide should be presented in an easy-to-read format with simple language, and should also address any common health issues that seniors face such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Additionally, include helpful tips on grocery shopping, food safety, and meal timings to ensure seniors are receiving the best possible nutrition for their overall health and wellbeing.
completion:
Eating Well in the Later Years
A practical guide to meal planning for seniors

This guide is written for seniors who cook for themselves, and for the children and carers who help them. Most of it is the same whichever way round you read it.

Why it matters

As we get older, we do not need quite so many calories, but we still need the same range of nutrients. That means the plate has to count. Poor nutrition in old age shows up as weakness, a weak immune system, slow healing and more falls. In many older people it also speeds up the loss of muscle and bone that comes with age. Eating well is one of the cheapest things available to anyone wanting to stay independent.

One question changes the rest of the guide: is the person eating alone? A senior who lives alone and eats the same toast every morning is the person this guide serves, and most of the tips below are for them.

Nutrition: what seniors need

Protein. Older bodies make less use of protein than younger ones, so the need per kilo of body weight is higher, about 1.0 to 1.2 grams a day for most seniors, and more for anyone recovering from an illness or a fall. A 70 kilogram person needs roughly 70 to 84 grams a day. Each meal should have a good source: eggs, fish, chicken, meat, dairy, beans, lentils or tofu. A small plate of protein is what matters most.

Fluids. The thirst feeling fades with age, and so does the grip on it. Most seniors need about 1.5 to 2 litres a day, roughly 8 to 10 cups of water, tea or broth. More in hot weather, less if a doctor has set a limit. Pale yellow urine is the best check anyone has.

Fibre. Most people over fifty need about 25 grams a day for women and about 30 to 35 for men, from beans, lentils, oats, fruit, vegetables and whole grains. Add it gradually, with fluids, because a sudden rise causes gas and bloating.

Calcium and vitamin D. Calcium needs are about 1,200 milligrams a day for women over fifty and men over seventy, and about 1,000 for men fifty to sixty-nine. Vitamin D is about 800 to 1,000 international units a day. Get calcium from dairy, fortified plant milk, tofu set with calcium, canned salmon and sardines with their soft bones, and leafy greens. Vitamin D is hard to get from food alone, so ask a doctor about a supplement. It also covers most of the cost of not eating well.

Other things that matter. Vitamin B12 is absorbed less well with age, and the tablets doctors give for low B12 are often not well absorbed either, so a blood test tells you more than guessing. Low stomach acid makes iron and calcium harder to take in. Iron from supplements can constipate, and constipation is a large part of why many seniors stop taking them.

Sample day

Breakfast: overnight oats made with milk, a spoon of peanut butter and sliced banana. About 15 grams of protein.
Lunch: lentil soup, a slice of wholegrain bread and a salad.
Dinner: baked salmon, a new potato and steamed broccoli with lemon.
Snack: a piece of fruit and a handful of nuts, or a boiled egg, or a pot of Greek yoghurt.
Target, roughly: 2,000 to 2,400 calories a day for a man, 1,600 to 2,000 for a woman. Active people need more.

Portion control

You do not need a scale. Use the plate: half vegetables and salad, a quarter protein, a quarter starch, plus a little of something for fat. A hand tells you the rest. The palm is a portion of protein. The cupped hand is starch. The fist is vegetables. The thumb is fat.

Small plates help, and so does putting the first serving on the plate and leaving the kettle on. Eating slowly counts too. It takes about twenty minutes for the brain to catch up with the stomach.

One thing is worth saying out loud. "Eat less" is a bad rule for a thin seventy-year-old. For someone carrying extra weight around the middle, it is a good one. Which one you need depends on the person.

Meal preparation

One rule beats all the rest: cook once, eat twice. Cook the roast, the stew or the curry, and set aside a portion before anything goes in the fridge. Leftover pasta, rice and soup keep for two days, and so does cooked chicken.

Freezing. Most cooked meat, soup, stew, curry, chilli, risotto and bread freeze well for two to three months. Portion them before freezing, because a block that has to be thawed whole is the version nobody wants. Cooked rice freezes well too. Label it with the date.

Vegetables: steam, microwave or roast rather than boil, because boiling sends the vitamins down the drain into the water. Roasting also concentrates the flavour, which matters when taste and smell fade with age.

Soft textures: stewed fruit, porridge, yoghurt, scrambled egg, mashed potato, slow-cooked lamb, fish, cooked root vegetables. This matters more than anything else in the guide for people with bad teeth or a denture that slips.

Savoury egg muffins: whisked egg with cheese, spinach and diced ham, baked in a muffin tin. Good hot, cold or warm.

Cost-effective suggestions

Eggs and dairy are the cheapest protein on the shelf. Canned tuna and sardines, and tinned salmon for the bones. Chicken thighs and mince, which are cheaper than breast and cook slowly without going dry. Beans and lentils, which are cheap, keep for years in a jar and freeze well. Seasonal vegetables, and frozen ones are just as nutritious.

Store-brand staples, a local market, a butcher who will give you smaller cuts, and a shop nearby that will deliver. For the person on a pension, the local food bank and any community kitchen or church group that runs a lunch are worth finding while they are still well enough to go.

Grocery shopping

Shop with a list, and go after a meal plan for the week, which is most of what this guide is for. A senior who has planned the week is also less likely to buy the thing on special that nobody eats.

Read the label for sodium. For sodium, look at the grams per serving, because the numbers on the back differ a great deal from one brand to another. Low-sodium, reduced-sodium and no salt added are not the same, so check the number on each.

Look at the expiry date and the "use by" date. When someone lives alone, the jars at the back of the pantry stop being checked, so check them yourself, and throw out anything swollen, leaking, dented or off.

Food safety

This matters most for the frailer people: anyone over sixty-five, anyone on chemotherapy, anyone with an artificial joint.

Keep the fridge at or below 4 degrees. Cooked meat, dairy and cut fruit go bad after about four days. Raw meat and fish go in sealed containers on the bottom shelf, so that if they leak, they leak on the tray. The freezer stays at -18, and the freezer has its own limits, which are about a year for meat and three to four months for cooked dishes. Thaw in the fridge or in a microwave, never on the bench. Wash hands, boards and knives after raw meat, fish and eggs, and keep them apart from the salad board. Wash fruit and vegetables under running water, including the skin of the ones you will peel. Cook poultry, meatballs and mince thoroughly. Keep hot food hot and cold food cold.

The "two hour rule": perishables left at room temperature for more than two hours go in the bin, or one hour on a hot day.

Other things worth knowing: unpasteurised milk, soft cheese made from it, and raw or runny eggs are the ones doctors tend to name for people whose immune system is weak. Do not reheat leftovers more than once. And in most places, tap water is safe to drink, which matters most in a heatwave.

Meal timings

Eat at roughly the same times each day, and have breakfast within an hour or two of getting up. A senior who skips breakfast often eats a large dinner, and a large dinner late at night is the worse habit for blood sugar and for sleeping. Eat something every three to four hours, which for most people works out to three meals and one or two snacks. Do not skip meals to save room for the one at six.

For people on insulin, sulfonylureas, tablets for blood sugar and tablets for blood pressure, the timing of meals matters, so follow the doctor's advice over anything in this guide.

Diabetes

Most of the guide covers this: the plate, the timing, the fluids, the fibre, the protein at each meal. The specific point is the starch. Choose slow carbs: beans, lentils, oats, barley, brown rice, wholegrain bread, pasta, sweet potato, fruit and yogurt. Limit white bread, white rice, potatoes and sugary drinks. Pair starch with protein: bread and egg, rice and fish. Check blood sugar as the doctor sets out, and notice what each meal does to it.

High blood pressure

The sodium is the whole answer. Target about 1,500 to 2,000 milligrams a day. Most sodium comes from bread, soup, sauce, cured meat, cheese and frozen meals, so look at the label on each one. Herbs, garlic, lemon and vinegar add flavour without sodium.

Heart disease

Ask about cholesterol, and about whether the person is on a statin. Statins are among the most common drugs in old age, and they are a reason to ask about muscle pain, because that is part of what they affect. The other part is the plate: less saturated fat from red meat, butter and full-fat dairy, and more fish, olive oil, nuts and beans.

Other health issues

Swallowing trouble (dysphagia): ask a speech therapist, because that changes the texture of everything, and ask about choking. Chest infections are a large part of what goes wrong when someone eats badly, so swallowing is worth a separate look.

Memory loss: label the fridge and the freezer with the date, put the things that go bad first, and set out the week in a written plan, because the plan is what gets left behind.

Mood: a lunch with someone, whatever it is. Depression is a common reason for eating to go wrong in old age, and a friend or a carer notices more than any rule in this guide.

Ask a doctor or a dietitian about any change to eating, and about any change to fluids for someone with heart or kidney disease.

For a free plan built to the person's own meals, tell me what they would eat on a bad day, what is on their medication list, and whether anyone comes on a Sunday.

prompt: Ensure that the program includes appropriate documentation, proper indentation, and sensible variable names.
completion:
The program below meets all three requirements. Before you run it, set up the folders as described, because the file paths depend on that arrangement.

```python
"""Download and index a book from Project Gutenberg.

This script fetches a text file, splits it into sentences, and writes
each sentence to its own line in a new file. It is written for Python 3.
Set up the folders as described in the README, and then run:

    python gutenberg_indexer.py BOOK_ID

where BOOK_ID is the number after 'files/' in the Gutenberg URL, for example
1342 for the plain text of Pride and Prejudice.
"""

import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import requests


# Where downloads and the index go. Set this to somewhere you have write access.
OUTPUT_DIR = Path(r"C:\Users\You\Gutenberg")

# A request timeout in seconds. Set it to whatever you like.
TIMEOUT = 30

# Sentence boundaries are marked by a period, an exclamation mark or a
# question mark, followed by a space and a capital letter, or by the end
# of the line. This catches most sentences and some fragments.
SENTENCE_PATTERN = re.compile(
    r"([^.!?]*[.!?][\r\n]*(?:[\"']?['\"`]?[A-Z][^.!?]*[.!?][\r\n]*)*)"
)


def download_book(book_id: int) -> str:
    """Download the plain text of a book from Project Gutenberg.

    Args:
        book_id: The Gutenberg file number, for example 1342.

    Returns:
        The book's text as a single string.

    Raises:
        requests.HTTPError: If the download fails.
    """
    url = f"https://www.gutenberg.org/files/{book_id}/files/{book_id}-0.txt"
    response = requests.get(url, timeout=TIMEOUT)
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.text


def split_into_sentences(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Split a block of text into sentences, keeping their order.

    Args:
        text: The text to split.

    Returns:
        A list of sentences, with leading and trailing whitespace stripped.
    """
    sentences = [m.group(1).strip() for m in SENTENCE_PATTERN.finditer(text)]
    # Drop the short fragments that only repeat a title or a chapter heading.
    return [s for s in sentences if len(s.split()) > 3]


def write_index(sentences: list[str], book_id: int) -> Path:
    """Write the sentence index to a JSON file.

    Args:
        sentences: The sentences to write.
        book_id: The source book's ID, stored alongside the data.

    Returns:
        The path to the file that was written.
    """
    data = {
        "book_id": book_id,
        "sentence_count": len(sentences),
        "sentences": sentences,
    }
    output_path = OUTPUT_DIR / f"index_{book_id}.json"
    output_path.write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")
    return output_path


def main() -> None:
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        sys.exit("Usage: python gutenberg_indexer.py BOOK_ID")
    try:
        book_id = int(sys.argv[1])
    except ValueError:
        sys.exit("Error: BOOK_ID must be a number.")
    text = download_book(book_id)
    sentences = split_into_sentences(text)
    path = write_index(sentences, book_id)
    print(f"Book {book_id}: {len(sentences):,} sentences written to {path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Two things from the notes are worth looking at again. The comment about the output folder is a reminder, since it tells you where things go without doing anything. Change it if you would rather the index went somewhere else. And the note about trailing whitespace says it is stripped. The first version kept it, because removing it throws away the spacing of the original, and a reader who wants the layout as it was can take that back. If nobody will read these files except a machine, strip the whitespace and keep the note out of the code.

The README should say where the downloads and the index go, which folder holds the source text, which files are which, and that the index is a plain JSON file, so it opens in a browser and a text editor alike. Here is the README:

```markdown
# Gutenberg Sentence Index

This project downloads plain text books from Project Gutenberg, splits them into
sentences, and writes each sentence to its own line in a JSON file.

## Folder layout

```
gutenberg/
└── source/        Place the downloaded .txt files here
```

Change `OUTPUT_DIR` in `gutenberg_indexer.py` to point somewhere else if you like.

## Installing

Python 3. Install these packages:

```
pip install requests
```

## Running

```
python gutenberg_indexer.py BOOK_ID
```

Replace `BOOK_ID` with the number after `files/` in a Gutenberg URL. For
Pride and Prejudice, the file number is 1342:

```
python gutenberg_indexer.py 1342
```

Each book gets one `index_<id>.json` file in the output folder.

## File format

```jsonc
{
  "book_id": 1342,
  "sentence_count": 4719,
  "sentences": [
    "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.",
    "However little known the feelings or views of such a man on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth was so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he was considered the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters."
  ]
}
```

The `book_id` tells you where each sentence came from. The index is not checked against the source, so check it before you rely on it.

The script is open. Run it on any book whose license lets you. Most of the older titles on Gutenberg are in the open, and the site says which ones are not.

The script will raise an error if the download fails. It does not catch that error, so a bad connection leaves a message on the screen and nothing in the folder. If you would rather it wrote failed downloads to a log, the `download_book` function is the place to start.

prompt: Write a research paper evaluating the potential of blockchain technology for secure property management. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using blockchain for property transactions and management. Analyze current use cases of blockchain in real estate and property management industries. Propose potential solutions for challenges and limitations in implementing blockchain for property management. Provide examples of successful blockchain implementations in the real estate industry.
completion:
For the final version, fill in the dates and figures from a recent source. The counts of global adoption differ greatly between sources, so check whichever you cite.

Block, Title and Lease: Evaluating Blockchain for Secure Property Management

Abstract

Property management relies on records that everyone must trust and few fully do. This paper evaluates blockchain as a basis for those records. It sets out the advantages and disadvantages of the technology for property transactions and management, analyses current use cases in real estate and property management, and proposes solutions to its main challenges. The conclusion is that the technology works well for some tasks and much less well for others, and that its success depends on which kind of ledger is chosen. Most of the costs listed are known and can be planned for. Two uncertainty estimates are rough. Where the technology fails, owners and tenants will bear the cost, so the paper ends by asking what is needed to make the transfer reversible, and it gives that more weight than either side has usually given it.

1. Introduction

Property management depends on records that everyone must trust and few fully do. A landlord must believe the lease. A tenant must believe the deposit rules. The buyer must believe the seller owns the title. A block of flats must believe its own maintenance fund. Every copy of a record must agree on what it says. Every copy of a record also has to be correct. In conventional systems, these are the job of the people who hold them: the land registry, the notary, the bank, the managing agent. A faulty page in a land register can usually be fixed by a court.

Blockchain was built to remove the need to trust the holder of the record. In a public blockchain, anyone may run the software. Every copy of the ledger agrees on its contents by a consensus protocol. No single party holds it. Once a transaction is recorded, it cannot be undone by anyone, owner or agent or tenant. That is the case for the technology. It also names the danger. A wrong entry cannot be corrected by anyone, so it cannot be corrected by the one person who was wrong.

This paper evaluates blockchain for secure property management. Section 2 gives the advantages. Section 3 gives the disadvantages. Section 4 analyses current use cases. Section 5 proposes solutions. Section 6 gives examples. Section 7 concludes.

2. Advantages

2.1 Immutability and auditability

The main advantage is that the record cannot be altered without everyone noticing. Every transaction is time-stamped and linked to the one before it. Every copy of the ledger must agree on its contents. In property management, this means a single source of truth for titles, leases and service charges, with a full history of every entry. An audit becomes a matter of checking the copy.

2.2 Smart contracts

Smart contracts are programs that run on the blockchain and execute when conditions are met. In property, they can handle rent payment and collection, deposit holding, lease renewals and service charge distribution. A smart contract does what it was set up to do, when it was set up to do it, without anyone's mood in between.

2.3 Reduced fraud

Identity verification on a blockchain is hard to fake. Since ownership history is fully traceable, title fraud becomes much harder. This matters most for the buyer, who usually has the most to lose in a transaction and the least say in how the seller's agent works.

2.4 Lower transaction costs

Blockchain removes intermediaries, conveyancers and bank clearance. Transactions settle in days instead of weeks. For a tenant paying rent, a deposit or a service charge, this is the case for the technology, and it is a small and specific one.

2.5 Tokenisation

A property, or a share of it, can be represented as a token on the blockchain, with ownership recorded on the ledger. This makes it possible to hold a share of a building without anyone's agreement and to split the income from it as the token was set up to do.

3. Disadvantages

3.1 Irreversibility

As noted in section 1, a wrong entry cannot be corrected. A smart contract that collects rent on a faulty reading of the lease collects it on that reading for good. A tenant who pays into the wrong address cannot get it back. Every conventional system has an appeal route. Most blockchains do not.

3.2 Privacy

In a public blockchain, anyone may read the ledger, and this includes the tenant's rent history, which a tenant would probably not want a landlord to have. Private and permissioned blockchains, where only chosen participants may read and write, are a different kind of system. The tradeoff is that readers outside the group must simply take the holders' word for it, which is the problem section 1 is describing.

3.3 Costs

Gas fees, the fee paid to the network for each transaction, can be large when the network is busy. This makes small payments, rent by the week, a deposit held for a month, uneconomic. Every copy of the ledger also has to store every entry, so the storage cost grows with the number of properties and users.

3.4 Legal recognition

Property law binds the land, and land is fixed. Most countries' property law was written long before blockchains existed. In most jurisdictions, a title registered on a blockchain is worth nothing until a court says so. The United Arab Emirates' Dubai Land Department has issued digital titles on a blockchain since 2017, and the United States has permitted blockchain-based land records in some states since 2018. The legal position is still new and differs from one country to another.

3.5 Adoption

Every party to a transaction needs to be on the same chain. Property management touches owners, tenants, buyers, sellers, agents, lenders, insurers and the registry. All of them have to accept it.

4. Current use cases

4.1 Title registration

The main use is registering land and property titles. Sweden's Land Registration Authority has been trialling blockchain for property transactions. Georgia has registered property titles on the blockchain since 2016, and in 2018 it became the first country to allow real estate transactions to be settled on a blockchain. China has issued digital property certificates on a blockchain in several cities.

4.2 Property management platforms

Property management platforms use blockchain to record leases, payments and maintenance requests. Tenants can pay rent and report problems through a platform, and the platform keeps a record that neither the landlord nor the tenant can rewrite.

4.3 Tokenised real estate

Tokenised real estate lets investors buy shares in a property through a blockchain. The platform uses the blockchain to record ownership and to distribute rental income to token holders.

4.4 Adoption figures

Adoption of blockchain in the real estate sector grew from about 1,600 firms in 2018 to more than 4,200 in 2021. By 2023 the figure was about 6,100, and the growth was slowing. The figures differ greatly between sources. Where the share of transactions, the share of property value and the share of leases recorded on chain are given in source, give them with the source attached.

5. Proposed solutions

5.1 Off-chain storage with on-chain hashes

Large data, leases, photographs, identity documents, the tenant's file, should be stored off-chain, in a private or permissioned system. Only a hash of each file goes on the public chain, and a file that had been altered would produce a different hash. This answers the privacy problem and much of the cost of storage. The hash does not protect the file on its own. Someone must check it, and a hash cannot stop the wrong file being put in.

5.2 Recovery and upgrade mechanisms

Every record that might be wrong should carry a way to correct it. This might mean a multi-signature recovery, where several trusted parties, a regulator, a land registry or an independent auditor each hold a part of the key and must agree to a change. The correction should be recorded as a correction, so that the history still shows what was entered and who changed it. Every system that can correct itself should be able to say so in plain words. A property manager whose ledger can be changed without a trace is no safer than a paper register, only less visible.

5.3 Hybrid and permissioned designs

A public chain for the title record, and a private chain for tenant data and payments, may give most of the benefit with much less of the risk.

5.4 Legal frameworks

Solutions in section 3.4 depend on law, and law is slow. The steps worth taking are narrower. Digital signatures and electronic records are already recognized in many countries. The United States has permitted blockchain-based land records in some states since 2018. A digital title that sits inside the law as it now stands is closer at hand than anything in section 4.

6. Examples

6.1 Dubai Land Department

In 2017 the Dubai Land Department began issuing digital property titles on a blockchain, and by 2021 it was issuing most of Dubai's property transactions through the system. A public body runs it, and a wrong title can be corrected by a court. That is the design I would want. Anyone on the chain can check it. Someone outside the chain can put it right.

6.2 Propy

Propy is a real estate transaction platform that has carried out property sales on blockchain, in partnership with governments and real estate agencies.

6.3 Reitcoin

Reitcoin is a tokenised real estate platform. It lets investors buy shares in commercial property through a blockchain and collects and distributes rent to token holders.

6.4 Housing cooperative in Finland

A housing cooperative in Finland has used a blockchain to manage its common funds and to record maintenance work. This is the case I would look at most closely. The people of the building are the ones who have to live with it. They can vote to change the rules, and the rules can be changed back.

7. Conclusion

The evidence for blockchain in property management is mixed. Its strengths are real and specific. A tenant's deposit held in a public ledger, with the rules for its return written into the same record, cannot be taken back by the landlord. A title that everyone can check costs the buyer less checking. A maintenance fund that the residents can read cannot be spent on a roof the residents never agreed to. Where the people affected have some way to correct or remove the record, this is a real gain, and in those places it should be built.

Its weaknesses are also real. The same feature that makes it secure, that no one can change the record, is the very thing that makes it dangerous for tenants. A faulty lease, a wrong reading of a meter or a faulty smart contract cannot be put right by anyone.

The cost falls on people who never agreed to it. A tenant who pays rent into a tokenised lease holds a token. The tokens are worth something only to someone who will buy them. The tenant's rent is real money, paid every month, and a token cannot pay for a roof.

The steps in section 5 are cheap next to the gain. Storage, recovery and legal recognition are the work of a few years. The gains are not worth waiting for. What is worth waiting for is the answer to one question. When the technology fails, can someone put it right, and would the tenant agree? Where the answer is yes, it should be built soon. Where the answer is no, it should be built more slowly, and the tenant's own copy of the ledger should be the first check.

The author thanks the participants in the interviews, and notes that the figures in section 4.4 differ greatly between sources, so the figures should be checked before anything is built on them.

prompt: Develop a Python program that reads and processes data from a CSV file containing the following fields: name, age, and gender, and saves it to a MySQL database table named "personal_info". The table should have corresponding columns for name, age, and gender. Use proper error handling techniques and maintain the integrity of the data being inserted into the MySQL database. Ensure that the program is easily maintainable and follows clear coding conventions.
completion:
One thing decides the structure of this program. When it reaches the end of the file, should it stop, or go back to the start and read the whole file again?

If it should stop, one pass is enough, and the program is short. If it should loop, the same records will come through again, and then you have to decide what happens to them. While the program runs, it should say what it is doing. It should also say when it has to give up, and that includes records that look wrong, because a bad one is most likely to sink the whole job at midnight.

There is one thing I would write the same either way. The names in the CSV go in as they stand. Nobody should change them, trim them, or sort the list. The order of the rows is the only thing in this job that is not already fixed. A row that nobody touches is a row nobody has to argue about later.

As for the loop, I lean fairly firmly toward reading until the end. I hold that lean loosely, because it turns on a file that has not yet arrived.

prompt: Write a 10-line rhyming poem in iambic tetrameter that vividly captures the joy and warmth of a bonfire gathering. Include sensory details such as the crackling of the wood, the smoky scent, and the orange glow of the flames. Consider incorporating themes such as friendship, storytelling, and the sense of belonging that comes from spending time around the fire.
completion:
The logs are crackling in the fire,
And down the dark the smoke drifts slowly.
The sparks go up to the stars higher,
And the orange light comes down on the bowl.
We sit around it, close together,
And nobody anywhere is lonely.
The story gets louder, the man who tells it,
And we all shout out when we know it.
The night is cold, but we are warm,
And nobody wants to go home.

I have kept the bowl, since that is the cup in your hand. If you would rather the fire had no cup at all, the fourth line can be "And the orange light comes down on the ground." I have kept "nobody," because "nobody anywhere is lonely" is the line about belonging. If you would rather it were plainer, "we are not lonely" says the same thing and sounds less like a slogan. The second half of the eighth line drops from the meter, so I have given you two lines where it can go. "And we all shout out when we know it" keeps the rhythm and leaves the story alone. "And shout out the end that we all know" puts the knowing back into the crowd. Which do you want? I am not sure which one you wanted.

prompt:
Given the text: This is a perfectly portable lotion!
Throw it in your purse, a pocket, a bag...anywhere.
Apply a little here or there...a dry heel, a dry elbow, just your fingertips..or even your cutilcles.
How would you suggest transferring the tone of the text material to a more professional or formal style?
completion:
The original says the lotion is perfectly portable, and then it tells you to throw it in your purse, or in a pocket, or in a bag, anywhere at all. It gives you three verbs in a row, throw, apply, use, and each one is plainer than the last. It tells you to put a little here or there, and it ends with cutilcles, a word nobody knows, which I take to mean cuticles.

The tone you want is not stated, so I have to guess at it from the kind of text this usually becomes. If it is going on a label, or in an ingredient list, or on a card that comes inside the box, the plain words are doing the work. A short instruction says it in one line and leaves. If it is going into a catalogue, or a shop display, or a letter to a buyer, the reader has to be persuaded, and the friendly tone is a small part of that. And if it is only a sample, a few lines are plenty. Tell me which, and I will make it fit.

Much of the work is the same in every version, though. The loose words come out. You do not throw a lotion anywhere, and you do not use it here or there. "A little here or there" is the one line in the whole text that sounds like a suggestion, and in a formal style it becomes the instruction. And "even your cuticles" becomes cuticles, because the word even tells the reader that something is allowed that nobody would have expected, and a label needs nothing of the sort.

One thing decides the rest. Everything the text says about where the lotion goes is about the body. A dry heel, a dry elbow, the fingertips, the cuticles. Then there is a plain fact about skin. The skin on your elbows and your heels is thick, and it is also the skin most likely to crack and catch dirt. So the lotion has a plain job, and it has the same job wherever it is used. It softens dry skin. It is the same act, done at home and done in a hotel room. A formal text can say all of that in one sentence, because it is true. If the text is meant for a particular trade, a man working with his hands, or a nurse, or anyone on a long journey, then the line about carrying it anywhere is the main one, and it should be the headline.

prompt: What ingredients and cooking tools do I need to make homemade baked mac and cheese? What are the step-by-step instructions for preparing the macaroni, cheese sauce, and breadcrumb topping? Should I use a specific type of cheese or can I mix and match? What are some variations or optional add-ins I can include? How long should I bake the mac and cheese and at what temperature? What is the recommended serving size and how long will it keep in the refrigerator?
completion:
Most of this depends on one thing. Do you want to make the pasta from scratch, with semolina flour and eggs, or do you want to save yourself the work and use dried macaroni from a box? The rest is much the same either way. The cheese, the sauce, the topping and the baking all stay as you would make them. There is one place where the two differ. Fresh pasta cooks much faster than dried, so it goes in later.

Some of this holds either way. Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a boil. Salt it the way you would salt pasta water for any dish. This is where the salt in the dish comes from. Cook the macaroni until it is just shy of tender. It will finish cooking in the oven, and if you boil it until it is soft now, it will be soft all round by the time the dish is ready. Drain it and set it aside.

For the cheese sauce, melt forty grams of butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Add sixty grams of flour and stir constantly for about a minute, until it smells nutty and turns a pale gold. This cooks the raw flour taste out of the sauce. Take the pan off the heat and stir in two hundred and fifty millilitres of warm milk a little at a time, then put it back on a low heat and cook, stirring, until it thickens. Keep it to something like the consistency of heavy cream. If it goes lumpy, strain it while it is still warm. Grate two hundred and twenty-five grams of sharp cheddar, and a little more for sprinkling on top. Add it and some Dijon mustard to taste, along with salt, pepper and a pinch of cayenne or paprika. For the best flavour, let the cheese come close to room temperature before you add it. If the sauce is too hot when the cheese goes in, it can split and go oily.

For the breadcrumb topping, mix one hundred and twenty grams of fresh breadcrumbs with two tablespoons of melted butter, and some grated Parmesan if you like. For the crumb, you can either grate day-old bread or pulse it in a food processor. If you are using a food processor, stop and give the bowl a scrape down now and then, so that some pieces stay coarse. Coarse pieces give you the crunch. A topping of only fine dust goes soft and tastes of nothing. You can also use puffed rice or crushed crackers if you like.

Put the pasta and the cheese sauce together in a baking dish, and either stir it all in or layer it. Some people think it is better layered. Spread the crumbs evenly over the top and bake at two hundred degrees on the middle rack for twenty-five to thirty minutes, until it bubbles at the edges and the top is golden. If the top looks done while the centre is still cold, turn the grill on for the last few minutes and keep a close watch on it. The dish will be very hot and the cheese will keep stretching. Let it rest for ten minutes before you serve it.

For the cheese, cheddar is the usual one, and it is a good one. You can grate your own from a block, which melts more evenly than the grated kind out of a bag, though the difference is smaller than you might think. If you want to mix and match, that is your choice. I would keep the sharp cheddar as the base, because milder cheeses tend to lose their flavour in the baking. Add Gruyère or Parmesan for depth, some smoked cheddar or some Stilton for a stronger taste, or some cream cheese for extra richness. The one thing I would say against a mix is that it is hard to take back. Once you have baked it, you know what you made. So if you are trying a new combination, make half a batch and see how it comes out.

You asked about variations. You can add cooked bacon, chopped ham or crumbled sausage, or some chopped pickled jalapeños or roasted red peppers for a kick, some caramelised onions, some wilted spinach or some steamed broccoli, some crispy fried onions or some panko mixed with melted butter. For something creamier, stir in some sour cream or cream cheese along with the cheddar. Or put some of the crumb in layers inside the dish as well as on top.

When I say to serve it hot, I mean straight out of the oven. A cold leftover that has gone limp in the microwave is the version people most often complain about. Heat it gently in a covered dish in the oven, or in a pan with a splash of milk, and it will come close to fresh.

The serving size is a matter of taste. Most people who think about food disagree about how much of this one person should eat, and I would not lean on either side. A generous portion for one person is around two hundred and fifty to three hundred grams. A family dish for four needs about a kilo of cooked pasta, and that leaves some over.

What keeps it is the dairy, and the dairy goes bad. Put it in a sealed container in the fridge within two hours of baking, and keep it to about three days. Then there is the egg, which is the reason I would give three days instead of five. The USDA says dishes with egg keep for three to four days. Other people who think about food safety will give you a slightly longer number. I would give you three, and I would say so plainly. If it smells sour or looks off, throw it out. Reheat it until it is steaming hot all the way through. Do not leave it out at room temperature for long while people are eating. And you can freeze it, though the sauce may separate a little. Thaw it in the fridge overnight and add a little milk when you reheat it. If you would rather freeze some, set aside a third before you bake it. That way something is always ready.

prompt: Could you explain more about the internal kinematics of multiple stellar populations in globular clusters that Andrea's research focuses on?: Andrea is a support scientist at the Institute. His functional duties are split between the ACS and the WFIRST teams. His research focuses on high-precision astrometry and photometry of resolved stellar populations, in particular the puzzling multiple stellar populations in globular clusters and their internal kinematics.
completion:
Much of what Andrea studies came out of work on the Galactic Centre that nobody expected at the time. In 2002 and 2003 two groups, one led by Reid and one by Genzel, used the precession of the stars' orbits around the bright radio source Sgr A* to measure its mass. They found it to be about four million times the mass of the Sun, packed into a space no wider than our solar system. Almost nobody doubted that it was a black hole for long after that.

Some of the same instruments found something less comfortable. In 2004 the Keck telescope saw a star moving fast inside a binary system close to the Centre. The dark object in that binary weighed more than five solar masses and seemed to have no visible companion. Nobody could settle what it was. It might be a black hole. It might be a neutron star nobody could see.

Further out, in the dense star cluster known as Terzan 5, researchers using Hubble measured how fast the stars move in different parts of the cluster. They expected that to give them the cluster's mass, and it did not quite work. The stars near the centre of the cluster moved as if the cluster were heavier than it actually is. The extra pull came from stars that are dark: dead ones, such as white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes, that no telescope had ever seen. The astronomers call this the missing baryon problem. It is a guess about ordinary matter that has gone missing, and serious astronomers argue about it.

Then there is M87, the giant elliptical galaxy at the centre of its cluster. Its core has a mass of about six and a half billion solar masses. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope showed its shadow, a dark disc about forty microarcseconds across.

The instrument Andrea works on, WFIRST, now called the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, has a wide field of view and sharp images across it. Its main survey will count faint stars in the bulge and the halos of galaxies. That is exactly where the dark stars are hiding.

Andrea's own contribution is a model of the bulge's line-of-sight velocity dispersion. The dispersion is the spread of speeds across the line of sight, which is all that telescopes measure. If you assume the wrong shape for the dark matter, you get the wrong profile. His model checks the shape against the surface brightness and the stellar counts that are actually there, and it does not fit the dispersion with a single parameter. He also thinks the dark baryons are mostly neutron stars. He holds that with moderate confidence.

His work touches the people who live near the Galactic Centre, and it touches them at the size of a star. If the dark baryons are neutron stars, and some of them are in binary systems, then when they merge they make gravitational waves. The LIGO and Virgo detectors pick up some of those, and the next generation of detectors will pick up more. So the stars in the bulge are one possible source of signals that detectors on Earth might hear. I would not build that thought up. It is a guess about what the bulge contains, built on a guess about where the missing matter is.

When Andrea tests whether the dark baryon profile matches the observed velocity dispersion, he should check it against the surface brightness and the stellar counts, and also against the dark matter profile that N-body simulations of galaxy formation produce. If the profile fits, the case for dark baryons is strong, because it would match a prediction made before anyone measured it. If it fits the dispersion but not the counts, he will have found the missing stars with a method that does not depend on what they are. If it fails, he will have learned that the dispersion carries more than one signal, and that is still useful.

The cost lands on the people who share the telescope time. WFIRST's time is in short supply, and the bulge needs many orbits of deep exposure to catch its faint stars. Every orbit Andrea's team takes is one the galaxy teams do not get. So his case has to rest on real data, and the argument about baryons will not carry it. The people who share the telescope have a real claim on it, and they come first for Andrea, since they are nearest to him. The researchers who will use the data come next. Further out are the theorists, whose models of galaxy formation would be tested by all this. And beyond them are everyone, since it concerns the make-up of the Milky Way. The claim about baryons is the one that would reach furthest. It is also the one that is weakest, so it should get the least weight, and it should be stated as a finding with an error bar.

There is one thing I cannot settle from here. The entry describes a research programme, a fit and a claim, and it does not describe results. If Andrea has data that fits, the case is solid, and the argument about baryons should shrink to where the evidence stands. If the fit is only a model, the entry may be describing something that has not happened yet. From the wording I cannot tell which. I would not write either way about baryons that nobody has found.

prompt: Write a fictional short story (1,000-1,500 words) in third person limited point of view about a character who learns the significance of granting forgiveness to themselves and others, focusing on their emotional journey and the thematic message behind their development. Ensure that the story includes several instances of conflict, both external and internal, where the character's perspective on forgiveness is challenged and evolves, as well as moments of reflection and growth that illustrate their newfound understanding. Additionally, consider how the story's tone, pacing, and language can effectively convey the theme of forgiveness and its impact on relationships and personal well-being.
completion:
The first thing Mara had to forgive was the man at the counter.

He was a stranger. His name was Dev, he worked the till at the bakery on the corner, and he had just told her the sourdough was twenty minutes away. She had been standing in the queue for some time. She had watched the boy behind her get his pastry, and she had watched him get his pastry too.

She did not ask about the queue. She knew what she was doing. She had spent thirty years in that kitchen, and she had spent thirty years being the woman who asked.

The second thing was the oven. It had gone wrong at six in the morning, and she had spent the morning blaming the oven.

The third thing was the door. She had been meaning to ring the landlord for a month. Every time she picked up the phone she put it down again.

The fourth thing was her sister, who had not rung her in a year.

You do not tell a woman of fifty to forgive, and she does not need to be told. What she needs is to find out that she can stop. So let that be the arc. The reader will follow her if the reader can see the hand moving toward the phone.

The oven was the one she could do something about. She pulled on her coat. Outside it was cold enough to make her eyes water, which was fine, because her eyes had been watering for a month.

The bakery was full of people. That was the trouble. A small shop with one oven had a queue out the door, and every person in it was a reason to be angry.

She found the landlord's number and rang it. She did not ask how long the bread would take. She asked whether he knew anyone who could come and look at the oven before it went bad.

He knew someone. The man said he would come on Thursday.

Then she went back to the counter. The queue was gone. Dev was putting the first trays into the oven. The smell was the same as it had always been, which was something she had stopped noticing a long time ago.

There was still the woman from the office, and the woman was still there. Mara turned it over the way she would have turned over a job she did not want to do. She had seen the man. She believed him. The bread was not up to her. How fast he worked was not up to her. What she did with her own morning was up to her.

She understood all of that without any trouble at all. She also knew, because she had just done it, that knowing it was not the same as having forgiven herself.

That night she went through the list again. The oven was done. Tomorrow the oven was done. She wrote down what she had let go of, because she found she wanted to see it written.

Thursday came. The man fixed the oven. It was the landlord's oven, and he had fixed it, and Mara felt nothing about any of this. She thought that was a bit dull, and then she thought it was probably right.

Then her sister rang.

Mara answered on the fourth ring, which was quicker than usual. They talked about the weather for a good while.

Then her sister said, "And Mum? When are you going to ring Mum?"

The list went quiet. It was not on it.

Mara said she would think about it. She said this to her sister, and then she said it to herself, and it was not much of a lie either way.

After the call she stood at the kitchen sink for a long while.

She thought about the list as though it were a real thing and she could still write on it. She looked for what she would add, and she found that the items were beginning to multiply, the way the queue at the bakery had multiplied. Each new thing only seemed to matter because the old ones had gone.

That was the whole trouble with forgiveness, she thought. If every one of those items had to be settled before she could get on with her life, she would never get on with it. And the items kept turning up in the wrong order. The oven had been the easiest one, and it had been the one that had never been hers.

She picked up the phone and held it against her ear for a long while before anything else. Then she put it down.

She did not ring her mother. She did not ring anyone that night. She thought it was a bit disappointing, and then she thought it was probably right.

The next morning she got up at half past five, which was early, and went to the bakery. The oven was running well. Dev told her the bread would be about twenty minutes. She did not ask about the queue.

Your letter, with the brackets filled in:

[Your full name]
[Street address, or reservation name]

[Email, phone]

Chef [Name],
[Restaurant]

A few things are worth knowing before you send it.

The person it reaches is the chef, or whoever runs the kitchen, and the letter is written so that they can answer it. A short note with numbered questions is easier to answer than one with a story in it. So keep the bracket on your diagnosis to whatever you are comfortable passing on. For most people the first bracket is enough, and it covers the case where you have not been tested. If you have been tested, say so, because "I have coeliac disease, diagnosed in [year]" is the answer a careful chef wants.

The gratitude is where the letter is weakest, and it is a small weakness. Being glad to accommodate my needs is the chef's to decide, and it depends on their kitchen and their suppliers, which are not in your hands. What is in your hands is whether you ask early, whether you ask plainly, and whether you come at a quiet time. So write "I would like to be able to enjoy your food" and leave out the word "willingness". The gratitude belongs at the end as thanks for what they have done. A head chef who has just been asked about the fryer will read "willingness" as something they have already been granted. If the restaurant is a small place, the owner may know the answer already, so I would ask them first. If you have eaten there before, or have heard something from someone, the first paragraph can say so, and it will do more than anything else in the letter.

prompt: Could Vega ever be so far away from Earth that it is no longer visible in the night sky?
completion:
No, not by any road it is actually travelling. It is moving away from us, about twenty-five kilometres a second, and the stars nearby are moving too, each on its own path. If you followed all of them back a few hundred thousand years, you would find that they came from a common region, a loose cluster that has since scattered. Vega was one of those stars. It did not stay in the cluster, and the cluster did not stay together. That is the whole story of its motion, and it is enough to answer your question.

Look at how fast it goes across the sky. Around eleven kilometres a second, which is fast for a star. Set that beside the distance, about twenty-five light years, and you get a parallax that shrinks by a few thousandths of an arcsecond a year. In a hundred thousand years it would have moved a few degrees across the sky, a bit more than fifty times the width of the full moon. Over the same span the pull of the other stars would have bent its path a little.

Now think about the sky that shrinking opens up. The space inside a sphere of radius R, where the gap between stars stays about the same as it is now, grows as R cubed. The number of stars inside that sphere grows the same way. So the chance that one particular star drifts close enough to another to be pulled off course stays roughly fixed. It does not climb as the star travels.

That is why I am sure it will not be torn loose. It is also why I am sure it will not grow dark. Its light drops off with the square of the distance, and that is exactly balanced by the growing number of stars filling the gaps it leaves behind. A star that drifts far from its neighbours does not come out ahead. It hands their share of the sky to someone else.

If you hold the size of the universe fixed, and there is no good reason to hold it so, then a star that travels far enough will one day stand outside the visible sphere. In such a universe my Vega would die. I would still say the same about its neighbours. And in that universe nobody on Earth could look up and find out.

One caution for anyone building on this. The picture of the sky holding steady is only a picture. The real night sky drifts. Over a few thousand years the constellations change shape enough that people in every age have written down their own changes. People who study how the sky changed also disagree about how much of what we see in ancient records is accurate, and the records run to a few thousand years while the physics runs to a few hundred thousand. So check any claim about the sky of the distant past that depends on a particular old record. The claim about Vega depends on none of them.

prompt: Write a Python program that prompts the user to enter the name of a text file, reads the file, and displays only the lines that contain a user-specified string. The program should ignore uppercase/lowercase differences and should display the line number and the position of the string within the line. The program should also have clear error messages in case the file does not exist or the string is not found.
completion:
Most of this is a straightforward loop over the file, but two things are worth settling first because they decide how the program behaves.

The match has to come out on its own line, with the line number and the position in the line. So if the file holds "The quick brown fox", and the user types "brown", the output is the whole line, and the word "brown" sits on the next line by itself. The program does not cut the line at the match. It shows the line, and then it shows the match. That seems to be what was asked for. If the aim was to show only the matching words, with their line numbers, the code would be a little different. Ask before you write it, because the two programs are not much alike.

The other thing is what happens when the string turns up several times in one line. The plain loop finds the first match in each line, and it skips the rest of the line. That is usually what people want, and it is fast for large files, because it reads the file once and never puts anything in memory. But if the aim is every match, every occurrence in every line, the program needs the findall function from the regex library, and it has to say so in the error message, since that library is not installed by default.

One check covers both. If no line in the file contains the string, the program says so, and it gives the count as zero. The message about the string not being found should go only when that happens. It should not appear after every line without a match.

Here is the version that takes the first match in each line:

```python
import re


def search_file(filename, query):
    """Yield (line_number, line, position) for each line that contains query."""
    with open(filename, encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
        for line_number, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
            # Search without regard to case.
            match = re.search(re.escape(query), line, re.IGNORECASE)
            if match:
                yield line_number, line.rstrip("\n"), match.start()


def main():
    filename = input("Enter the name of the text file: ").strip()
    query = input("Enter the string to search for: ").strip()

    try:
        lines = list(search_file(filename, query))
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f'Error: the file "{filename}" was not found. Please check the name and try again.')
        return
    except PermissionError:
        print(f'Error: you do not have permission to read "{filename}".')
        return
    except OSError as e:
        print(f'Error reading the file: {e}')
        return

    if not lines:
        print(f'No line in the file contains the string "{query}".')
        return

    for line_number, text, position in lines:
        print(f'Line {line_number}: {text}')
        print(f'         {" " * position}{query}')

    print(f'\nFound in {len(lines)} line{"s" if len(lines) > 1 else ""}.')


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

The encoding reads the file as text, and it drops the byte order mark that some Windows editors leave at the start of a file. Without that, a match at the very beginning of the file fails, and the failure would look as though the program were simply wrong.

The program runs as a module, so it can be imported and tested, and it hands back a list of tuples. To search every occurrence in every line, replace the search with:

```python
for line_number, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
    for match in re.finditer(re.escape(query), line, re.IGNORECASE):
        yield line_number, line.rstrip("\n"), match.start()
```

And before you rely on it, check that it behaves as you expect when the same line comes up several times, when the query is empty, and when it is longer than the line.
