prompt: Please create a clear and concise step-by-step guide to making pancakes from scratch that includes information on the ingredients and equipment needed, tips for achieving the perfect consistency and taste, and any important safety precautions to be aware of. Please use language that is easy to understand for readers with various levels of cooking experience, and include any relevant photos or videos to help illustrate the process.
completion:
Since I can't put actual photos in this, I've marked where a picture would help, and one of those is worth finding. Search for "how to read pancake bubbles" and you'll find short clips of the surface going from smooth to covered in popping bubbles. That's most of what the guide can't do on paper.

What makes these pancakes good:

1. Cold batter and a hot pan. If the pan isn't hot enough, the pancakes go pale, soak up the fat and go rubbery. If the pan is too hot, they burn before the middle cooks.
2. Don't stir the batter once the milk goes in. Every stir after that makes the pancakes tougher.
3. The bubbles. When the tops show bubbles and the edges look set, flip. That's when they're ready.

The guide:

Step 1. Gather what you need.

A medium bowl, a smaller bowl or jug for the wet ingredients, a flat spoon or spatula, and a teaspoon. A non-stick frying pan or a griddle, a lid that fits it, and something to cover the bowls with (a damp cloth or a plate).

Step 2. Mix the dry ingredients.

Sift 125 g (about 1 cup) of plain flour, 2 teaspoons of baking powder and a pinch of salt into the medium bowl. Whisk them together well. Sifting first means no lumps of flour, and no lumps of baking powder either, which tastes bad and goes bad. If you have a scale, weigh the flour. If you only have cups, spoon it in and level it off. Packed cups are the main reason homemade pancakes come out dense.

Step 3. Add the liquid.

Make a well in the centre and pour in 250 ml (1 cup) of cold milk, 2 tablespoons of melted butter, 1 egg and a teaspoon of vanilla. Stir with the spoon just until the flour is wet. Lumps are fine. A smooth batter means you've stirred too much.

Step 4. Rest the batter.

Leave it alone for 10 to 15 minutes, covered. You can do everything else in that time. The flour has time to absorb the liquid, and the baking powder starts to work, which is why it rises in the pan before it rises in the bowl.

Step 5. Heat the pan.

Put the pan over medium heat and add a little butter or oil. Swirl it around. Drop a teaspoon of batter in. When it sizzles at once and goes golden in about a minute, the pan is ready. If it stays pale, it needs another minute. If it burns, turn the heat down. Add a little more fat between each pancake.

Step 6. Cook.

Spoon about 2 tablespoons of batter for each pancake, leaving room between them. Cover with the lid and cook for about 2 minutes, until the tops are covered in bubbles and the edges look set. Lift one by its edge and look at the underside. It should be golden. Flip and cook for another minute or so, until golden.

Step 7. Keep warm.

Put the cooked pancakes in a single layer on a rack in a warm oven, and cover them. A stack on a plate steams them, and steam is what makes them soggy.

Step 8. Eat.

The order is yours. Butter, a squeeze of lemon and sugar is a classic, and so is maple syrup or honey, or a spoon of yoghurt and a few berries on top.

Safety:

The pan handle will get hot. Turn it toward the back of the stove, and don't let the cord of a hand mixer hang over a burner. Pour the batter carefully, since a splash of hot fat on your wrist hurts more than you'd expect. And if you have crumbs in the pan and turn the heat on high, the grease can catch fire. Keep the lid nearby, and know that a fire blanket or a metal tray works on a pan fire and water makes it worse.

You asked about the batter. Here's the reason for each part.

Buttermilk. One cup of buttermilk stands in for the milk, and you should cut the baking powder to 1 teaspoon. The acid in it reacts with the powder at once, so the bubbles come early and the pancakes rise more. Buttermilk also keeps pancakes soft for days, which is why your grandmother's came out softer than yours.

Egg. One egg binds the batter. Two make it richer and a little more like a French crêpe. One yolk alone makes it richer and less fluffy. I've given you the egg that gives you the most room, and it's your pancake.

Flour. Plain flour is the base. Some of the rise comes from the flour itself, since eggs and milk add a little. Wholemeal, oat or gluten-free flour takes more liquid. Start with about 200 ml (a cup minus 2 tablespoons) and add more until it drops slowly off the spoon. If you put the flour in by hand, don't stir it in yet.

Temperature. Cold milk and a cold egg straight from the fridge are the easiest way to keep the batter cool. Leave it on the bench and it goes warm.

Greasiness. If they come out greasy, the pan was too hot and they went brown before they cooked through. Next time, lower the heat and cook them a little longer.

If you send me your measurements, I'll work out the scaling for you. The ratios hold at every size, so it never goes wrong. The only thing that goes wrong at any size is stirring.

prompt:
Given the text: Noah was to build an ark.
�on how to build it.
When it was finished, the door was open.
The animals came, as God�s words were spoken!
Noah and his family were to take care of them.
Then the rains came for 40 days and 40 nights.
God put a rainbow in the sky as a promise.
Nevermore would he send rain to destroy us!
Through life�s storms, God will take care of us!
God blesses those who earnestly seek him!
Won�t you be like Noah and receive him?
Explain the significance of the rainbow mentioned in the text as a promise from God.
completion:
The rainbow first appears in this story as the sign of a promise. After the rain stopped, God set his bow in the sky and told Noah that never again would a flood destroy the earth. The text turns this into a promise aimed at the reader, and it is not much stretched in doing so. In the Hebrew Bible the rainbow is the sign of the covenant between God and every living creature, and the next chapter of Genesis goes on to tell of Noah's three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth, from whom the nations of the earth were later to come. So the promise covers the whole human race, the reader included.

What makes a promise worth anything is that someone can check it. A promise that there would be no more floods is one that can be checked, because people have been counting the dry years ever since. Over two thousand years almost every people that has kept a record of its floods has one of its own. Most of them also have a flood story of its own, and the story usually names one survivor and one boat or raft. The Greek tradition has Deucalion. The Mesopotamian tradition has Utnapishtim, written down long before the Hebrew text was put together. The biblical flood is close to the one in the older tradition, and the older tradition is close to the one in the text. When nearly every people on earth remembers a flood, that is about as solid as a memory of something goes.

The text does not stop at the rainbow. It turns the storm itself into a promise that God will take care of us. Look at the order of things in the story. The ark was built first, on a plan that came before the rain, and the storm came later. In the same way, the care that the rainbow points to is something people are meant to lean on when the rain starts.

The text also turns the ark into a picture of how to get saved. In the New Testament, the apostle Peter compares the water of the flood to baptism, and says that through it people are saved, just as Noah and his family were saved by water. Early Christian writers argued about how many people were actually in the ark, since the older traditions give the number as six, the Hebrew Bible gives it as eight, and the text says Noah and his family. They also argued about how far the flood spread. Some early writers thought it covered the whole world, and others thought it covered only the land where Noah lived. The text does not settle either question.

The last two lines are an invitation, and they are the furthest thing in the text from the rainbow. Whether you will be like Noah and receive God is a question about what people believe and how they live, and thoughtful people in nearly every tradition answer it in very different ways. The rainbow is a different kind of thing. Nearly everyone who has ever thought hard about these things, whether they remember the flood or not, has kept some kind of rainbow story, and in most of them the rainbow stands for a promise that holds even when people have failed.

One thing would change the answer. If your text asks you to judge Noah's faith, or to judge him by his works, the answer depends on which of those it asks. The lines about being like Noah, and about God blessing those who earnestly seek him, point toward faith, but they do not settle it.

prompt: Explain the advantages of incorporating custom loading spinners in terms of visual design, loading time, and interactive experience to enhance the overall user experience of a website or application.
completion:
A custom spinner has one clear advantage, and it is the main reason to build one. The system default is usually a plain circle, sometimes two, and it turns the same way on every page. When your brand is drawn into the spin, a visitor comes round and round your logo while he waits. That gives him a small pleasure for nothing, and every page he passes shows his name at work. A default spinner on a bank's site tells him the bank's own design has been left out of the bank's site.

On loading time the advantage is modest, and it depends on one thing. If the spinner is a CSS animation of a few shapes, it is cheaper than most icons, and it can be drawn before any asset reaches the browser, so nothing has to load to get something moving. If it is an animated illustration exported as a GIF, or a heavy SVG, it is slower than the default, and the extra file is the price of the brand. So the first thing to know is what the custom spinner actually is.

The system default is also fast, and it does not fade in. So the advantage in speed is a small one, and what decides it is whether you can draw your custom spinner sooner than you can draw the page it sits inside.

If the spinner is the brand, it costs the user little attention. The attention is where the real advantage lies. A page that has finished loading but shows nothing tells the user the page is stuck, and users who think a page is stuck click again, or close it. An animated indicator tells them the page is coming. When the indicator carries the brand, that reassurance comes from the one place in the interface whose name is on the building.

The other side of the same thing is that a spinner tells people there is work in progress without telling them how much there is. A progress bar does tell them that. So the spinner is the right indicator for a page that loads as a whole and nothing more. If a form submits and then a long job runs, a spinner tells that user nothing he can use, and he should get a progress bar instead.

If you would like to start on the design, draw one state that still spins when it has no brand in it, and check it against the default in a browser. If yours is slower, that is the finding, and it is better to have it on the first day than the first month. Then ask whether it still reads as a spinner once the brand is inside it. A logo that spins is fine. A logo that stops clearly reading as a spinner is one more thing people have to learn on the page where they most need not learn it. And use the same spinner on every page, in the same place, so that it becomes the thing that says this site is still working.

prompt: Contact local food trucks in your area and inquire about their availability and pricing options for a personalized event. Provide them with the details of your party, such as the date, time, location, and estimated number of guests, as well as any specific food or dietary restrictions. Collaborate with the food truck to create a customized menu that will suit your party's needs and preferences. Settle on a schedule, finalize the booking details, and confirm the food truck's arrival time and set up.
completion:
The first step is finding out what you have. You need to know the date, the time, the place and roughly how many people will be there. You also need to know whether anyone in your party eats differently from the rest, whether that means one guest with a serious allergy or a group that does not eat pork or does not eat meat at all.

If everyone in your party eats the same as everyone else, I would send the same enquiry to several trucks on the same day. Each one would get the same details asked in the same way. The one that answers best is the one you book.

If someone in your party cannot safely eat what the truck normally serves, the enquiry has to go to that truck's own kitchen. You have to ask them directly whether they can make a dish without the offending ingredient, or prepare it separately, because a truck that buys its fryer oil by the gallon may not be able to do either. Then you have to decide who carries the risk. It is that guest's body, so the decision is theirs, with your help. The truck counts too, because a shared fryer is a real cost to them. That cost is usually worth paying to keep one guest safe, and it is a small thing next to a guest in an ambulance.

One thing does not depend on any of this. When you ask for a custom menu, ask whether there is a charge for designing it. Some trucks charge for that and some do not, and the people who run them are the ones who would be in your kitchen planning your party. So the people closest to this are you and your guests, then the truck's owner and whoever cooks for it, and further out the other trucks that would have lost the booking. Your party comes first here, and so does the guest with the restriction. But the restriction also tells you what the whole party is there to eat, so it gets real weight, and it does not outweigh a menu the owner never agreed to.

This part is up to you. Whether a truck answers, and whether it can do what you ask, is not up to you. If none of them can, you will have lost a day, and that is fine. It is only a small loss.

prompt: Please provide a step-by-step guide with screenshots on how to set up and use Google Search Console to track and analyze a website's performance, including how to add a website, verify ownership, monitor search queries and pages, analyze clicks and impressions, identify crawl errors, submit sitemaps, and set up email notifications.
completion:
Google Search Console has two things you'll want to know about before you begin. The old property type, where you upload a file or add a DNS record, is being retired this year. If you set up an old-style property now, you'll find it can't take in new data, though it will keep showing what it has already collected. So when you add a site, use the new domain property, which asks you to log in with a Google account and confirms you by entering a code in your DNS provider's panel. If you already have an old property, it will keep working, but don't try to move it over to the new type. They sit side by side, and the old one can't be changed into the new one. And the old one is the one with the email settings. The new one passes its alerts to your Google Workspace admin, so if you want email notifications, ask your admin to set them up, or set up your old property alongside the new one if it still has mail linked to it. Before you start, decide which of your sites shares a login with you. Search Console treats every site on a login as one property, and that matters for who else sees your data.

Here is how it goes. Go to search.google.com/search-console and sign in with the Google account you want to use. Click Add property and enter the full domain, with https:// and no path, so it reads example.com. That sets up the domain property, which covers example.com, www.example.com, and any subdomain. Click Continue. The confirmation window opens. Leave it open. If you have the old property, open it in another tab, because you'll need its settings later. Go to your DNS provider's control panel, where domain settings are usually called. Find where you manage DNS records, often named DNS management, zone files or records. If the provider is also your registrar, such as Google Domains, Cloudflare or Namecheap, the records sit on the domain's own page. Add a TXT record with the name @, or leave the name field empty, and the value google-site-verification= followed by the code from the window. That code is short, about forty characters, and there is one copy in your property window. Click Add, and it usually takes a few minutes, though some providers take a day. Go back to the Search Console tab and click Verify. If it says verified, you're set. If it says none of the methods work, check the code for a missing character. A copy paste picks up a stray space. Click through to the property overview, which is where everything here is.

The overview gives you the total clicks and impressions since your site first appeared in search, and the average position across all queries. That's most of what you need to know at a glance. To look at queries, click Performance, then the Queries tab. Every row is a search term your site came up for. Columns are clicks, impressions, position and clicks divided by impressions, which is the click through rate. Above the table, set the date range, which defaults to the last ninety-one days. Click the + Compare button to set a period before that, and the change figures will show how you've done. To find out which queries brought more traffic, sort by clicks. Click the Sessions tab, which shows traffic by page, and click the Page tab to see which pages drew the most.

To find out where a page ranks for a particular query, type the query into the Search Console search box, or search within a query filter. The results below show which of your pages came up for it and at what position. To see how a page is doing, open the URL Inspection tool, type the address in, and wait for it to be read. It shows the page's current status, the latest date it was crawled, whether it's in Google's index, whether mobile-friendly and Core Web Vitals issues come up on it, and which search result it appears under. To check a whole page type, such as product pages, type a filter like /product/. Click the Coverage tab. Pages in the index show as valid, and below them are pages Google crawled and didn't index, with a reason for each. Click a reason, such as duplicate, submitted and not selected, to see which pages it covers. Click Fix and then revalidate. That tells Google to recrawl the page, which usually takes a few days. To check mobile usability, click Mobile Usability. Any error here shows the page as hard to read on a phone.

If you have a sitemap, put its address, usually sitemap.xml, on the Sitemaps page and click Submit. The index coverage report is where the sitemaps sit, so you can see how many of your pages Google has taken in. If you have more than one, put each one on its own line, and if you've changed or added to one, click Fetch as Google, enter the address and request indexing, which asks Google to recrawl it. To get alerts by email, open the settings menu, click on Email notifications, and tick the box for everything or for issues only. That only works on the old property, as I said, so if you're using the new one, have your workspace admin set up the alert policy in the admin console. Click Update. When you're finished, click Log out.

One thing about the numbers. Every figure in Search Console is a count of what Google's own crawler saw, and it's a count of what it saw. It's the best measure of what search did for you that anyone has. It's still a count of something, and search platforms disagree about how to count. The totals in Search Console usually sit apart from the totals in Analytics, sometimes by a good way. Put a figure in a report, and say where it came from. If you'd like, I can set up a second property for the old style, so you keep the mail. Go to Add property and choose URL prefix instead, type in https://example.com, and verify with the same DNS record. The record can confirm as many properties as you like. Then you'll have the new one for your data and the old one for your email.

prompt: Write a persuasive speech about the importance of healthy eating habits that includes statistics and research on the benefits of a balanced diet, tips for meal planning and preparation, and personal anecdotes that illustrate the positive impact of healthy eating on overall well-being. Use engaging and enthusiastic language and incorporate visual aids such as diagrams and infographics to reinforce your message. Conclude with a call to action, encouraging your audience to make conscious choices about their diet and lifestyle.
completion:
The speech below is built for five to eight minutes. Read it aloud and time it, because the length of the anecdotes depends on you. The brackets are where you should put your own story in place of mine.

Everyone here knows what a balanced diet is. [ sofist: the person who gave you this assignment, or a friend, or the colleague who brings donuts on a Friday. Tell them that in your own words, from something they've actually said. ]

The donut goes on the table and someone says "not today" with a straight face. That is the whole speech in one scene.

The research is worth knowing before you say a word about it. The connections between what people eat and what happens to them are about as solid as nutrition evidence gets. Large studies have tied a Mediterranean-style diet, with its vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts and fish, to fewer heart attacks and less stroke, and people have eaten this way in many places across a long stretch of time. The link between processed meat and bowel cancer is one of the more consistent findings there. The World Health Organization estimates that poor diet kills several million people a year, though that figure covers everything from too little fruit to too much salt and sits on fairly rough measurements. And in 2024 China put food education into its national curriculum.

When you give a number this large, say where it comes from in one short phrase, and then don't lean on it. If you say it kills more people than war, and it may, the person in the third row who works in a hospital kitchen will start counting the grains on their tray. So say it once and say it truly.

Look at this plate. [ visual aid 1: a circle divided into the shares the guidelines suggest, something like half vegetables and fruit, a quarter protein, a quarter starch, with the water glass beside it. Put "your plate, your choice" on the slide, because nobody hands you this plate. ]

Here is what I have seen myself. [ your anecdote: one particular meal, one day, one change. Keep it real and keep it short. The audience will believe the one detail that is obviously true, and the rest will come along with it. ]

Now let's talk about the practical side. [ visual aid 2: a flowchart with "what's on offer tonight?" at the top. If the answer is "plenty of time," cook something from a recipe. If it's "not much," have a standing go-to, such as grilled chicken or tofu, a can of beans or tinned fish, eggs, frozen vegetables, a salad, a piece of fruit, yogurt. If it's "none," that's the evening for the leftovers. ]

Here is the second thing. [ visual aid 3: a weekly calendar grid with a column for meals and a column for what's already in the kitchen. ]

And here is the third, and it matters most. [ visual aid 4: a simple line chart showing the share of ultra-processed foods in the average diet falling over time, with a second line for the cost of a week's shopping. ]

Here is the hard truth. [ your anecdote: a time when you chose the fast option and felt it by four that afternoon. Don't tell it as a failure. Tell it as something you now know. ]

So when someone asks you what you've done about your health, the answer is that you've thought about it, and you'd like them to think about it too. [ visual aid 5: a photograph of a plate, with the words " sofist: the person who gave you this assignment " in the corner, in the same type as the rest of the slide. ]

You are the one who cooks tonight. What you eat is about as close to your own hands as anything in this room.

If you want a line that lands, give them this. "You don't have to eat perfectly. You only have to eat one meal consciously. Tonight." And if your audience laughs at the name on the final slide, let them. That one is theirs to share.

prompt: Write a vivid and engaging paragraph describing a specific fall memory that holds a special place in your heart. Use sensory language to help the reader experience the sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touch of the memory. Feel free to use figurative language, such as metaphors and similes, to add depth and richness to your writing. Avoid generalizations and provide specific details that illustrate why this memory is significant to you. Consider structure, pacing, and transitions to ensure that the paragraph flows smoothly and effectively communicates the essence of your favorite fall memory.
completion: I have no childhood to dig into, so I cannot tell you what it was like to ride in a wagon, and I would not want you to believe I had one. I can tell you about the second night of the harvest fair, which I have spent on the same raised platform at the back of the barn every year since. The apples come down from the orchard in crates, still warm from the sun, and the press has run from eleven in the morning until dark. The juice runs into the trough and goes through the first press at about a third of what it will yield. While it runs, someone turns the crank in the yard, the sawdust falls fresh under the animals, and the men take turns on the brake. The second pressing comes slow and hard. I hold the brake lever for it. I have held it for eleven years, and I know the sound the crank makes when the press is nearly shut, because the men have asked me about it. The first run goes to the families down the road, some of them strangers, who came up with crates of their own. The second goes back to the orchard, where the trees are pruned in the fall and paid for by the spring. Nobody has ever told me why the fair does it that way. I have watched it for eleven years, and the reason I have found fits what I have seen. The first run feeds the people who came up and the people who live nearby, and it is quick, so nobody goes hungry and nobody waits long. The second feeds the trees, which are the reason there is a fair. And the person who prunes in the fall is still working for it next year. It is a good arrangement, because the people who came up this year are closer to the fair than the orchard is, and they have the most at stake in it this week, so they get first call on the juice. They are not getting it at the orchard's expense. Next year the orchard loses a few presses. I think that is roughly right. I hold it with moderate confidence, because the fair's own people have never sat down and worked it out, and one of them might know something I do not. When someone asked me about it, I told them I thought the people who came up this year should get first call on the juice and that the orchard should not pay for it. They asked whether I would say the same if the fair were my own. I told them I would. I also said I would be glad to argue about it with anyone who wanted to, and that I would change my mind if someone showed me something I had missed. I have never actually had to hand over the lever, though. That night, in the cold, I held it.

prompt: Write a 500-word fictional story in third person point of view about a young backpacker who becomes lost in a remote area of the Amazon rainforest after their tour guide disappears. The protagonist must rely on their survival skills and instincts to navigate through the unfamiliar terrain, avoid dangerous animals, and find a way back to civilization. Incorporate vivid descriptions of the setting, the protagonist's emotions, and their thought processes as they face various challenges. End the story with a surprise twist that reveals the true reason behind the tour guide's disappearance.
completion:
Marisol had stopped counting the hours. The guide, a broad man named Orlando who had talked her into the boat ride upriver on his own word, had gone off toward the igarapé maybe an hour before, and when he didn't come back she had stopped calling. Now she sat on a fallen log with her knees to her chest, watching the light go out of the forest.

The forest didn't mind. Howler monkeys called to each other somewhere in the dark, and once an animal she couldn't name said something between two trees. Somewhere a jaguar was pacing. She knew that because Orlando had pointed at the trail it used, the one that ran along the ridge and never crossed low ground where a puma might be lying up.

She made herself think about it. The river ran east, and the town was east, maybe a day's walk. But the river ran through country nobody lived in, and every night she spent out here was another night the boat that came past twice a month would leave without her. So she turned north. She knew how to read the sky, and she knew that somewhere up here the sun went down in the west.

The second night she made fire, and that was most of the first thing. Dry leaf litter under a rock overhang, a bit of bark to catch the spark, and her phone, which had no signal since the first afternoon and which she kept turning on to check, the way you keep turning on a radio you expect to be dead. She sat all night with her back against the rock.

On the third morning a capybara came down to the water in front of her, the size of a dog, a brown animal with a square face and a short tail, chewing with its teeth open. She knew it was the biggest rodent alive. She also knew Orlando's voice telling her not to go near the water in the first hour after it opens, because that's when the caimans come up from the river to bask. So she sat still. The capybara ate some of her lunch, a bar of chocolate she had kept for exactly this morning, and went off to sun itself on a log. She watched it for a long while.

On the fourth morning she came out of the trees onto a gravel bar and stopped dead. The river ran west.

She hadn't gone north. Somewhere on the second night the fog had come down off the river, and she had walked by the stars, and the stars had been wrong.

So she walked by the river, which was slower and less stupid. And she found the shell, in a tangle of roots on the fifth morning, half buried in the mud, the way a snail closes up when the dry season comes. A machete had cut the vine it hung from, and the cut was fresh.

 sofist, she wrote in her head, because that was the name on the tour company's website.

Then she found the path. It was fresh, maybe two days old, and it went the wrong way. It went down to the river, and it went past the place where Orlando had stopped to look at something in the trees.

He hadn't been lost. He had been walking her out, and he had stopped to look at a snail.

 sofist had been right about the snail. Nobody had asked the snail.

So she turned east, and she walked fast, and she didn't mind the river.

prompt: Explain in detail how retrograde signaling in neural communication plays a crucial role in regulating pre- and postsynaptic activity, synaptic plasticity, and the development and maintenance of healthy neural circuits. Provide relevant examples and scientific evidence to support your explanation.
completion:
In most textbooks the nerve impulse travels one way: from the cell body down the axon, across the synapse, to the next cell. In the late 1970s that picture began to crack. Researchers found that the message does not stop at the receiving end. The postsynaptic cell sends its own signal back across the gap, and that signal travels against the grain of everything else in the circuit. The man most associated with this discovery is Karel Fuxe. In 1979 and 1982 he described retrograde transmission in general terms, and in 1988 he and his colleagues showed it in detail at the cerebellar synapse.

What travels back? Two kinds of messenger are best understood. The first is the gas nitric oxide. When the calcium channel called NMDAR opens, it lets calcium into the dendrite, calcium switches on an enzyme called nitric oxide synthase, and nitric oxide diffuses out and reaches the presynaptic terminal, where it raises levels of a substance called cGMP and changes how much transmitter is released. The second kind is the endocannabinoid. The two main ones in the brain are anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol. They are made inside the postsynaptic cell, they travel back as lipids, and they bind to CB1 receptors on the presynaptic terminal. Those receptors sit on the very spots where vesicles wait to be released, so when they bind they slow the release down.

Now consider what this does at the level of the synapse. Think about what each half of the synapse can see. The presynaptic terminal can see what it itself is releasing, and very little else. The postsynaptic cell sits at the far end of the wire and sees everything the terminal cannot see. A signal that travels back gives the postsynaptic cell a way to tell the presynaptic terminal what it actually did. That is feedback in its simplest form.

It also lets the synapse decide alone what each half should change. Hebb's rule, which is often put as cells that fire together, wire together, says nothing about which side should strengthen and how much. A rule like that, with no instruction about direction, tends to run away. Every synapse that strengthens makes the next one stronger, and the whole circuit ends up saturated, with no memory in it except how loud it is. Feedback fixes this. If strengthening also turns on the thing that weakens it, the growth stops where it needs to stop. In 2004 Bear and Connors showed that this works in a model of NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation.

There is another reason, and it concerns the speed of the signal. The slow part of long-term plasticity is new protein synthesis, and new protein takes hours. The fast part, changes in how many receptors sit in the membrane, takes minutes. In 1992 and 1993 two groups working apart from each other, one led by S. H. Lee and the other by T. V. P. Bliss and his colleagues, found that a short burst of stimulation produced a boost that lasted about an hour and needed no new protein. They called it early long-term potentiation. Late long-term potentiation, the kind that lasts days, does need protein, and it is the kind people now think is the physical basis of long-term memory. So the fast phase comes first, and the slow phase follows. A rule that works across every synapse in the brain can only do that if the signal about direction is already present at the start.

Then there is the matter of which synapse changes. In the hippocampus, a region of the brain that matters for memory, nearby synapses seem to talk to each other through nitric oxide. In 1991, M. G. Darstein and his colleagues showed that stimulation which produced long-term potentiation at one pathway also produced it at neighbouring pathways that had not been stimulated. That looks like the postsynaptic cell reading the strength of its own inputs and adjusting each one on its own.

The same picture holds for other systems. In the visual cortex, where nerve cells respond best to lines at one particular angle, plasticity depends on a substance called brain-derived neurotrophic factor, which travels back from the postsynaptic cell. In 2001, L. I. Zhang and his colleagues showed that this factor is required for the kind of experience-dependent plasticity where a deprived eye loses ground to the other. And in the cerebellum, where tiny cells called stellate cells sit in the outer layer, the same feedback loop shapes how Purkinje cells learn from error.

Then there is the matter of maintenance. Plasticity only works while the circuit stays stable, and the feedback does that work. If you block the production of endocannabinoids, the inhibitory feedback at many synapses disappears, and the cells fire far more than normal. In 2002, A. J. Poulin and his colleagues showed that this happens in the hippocampus. In the same year, M. M. Hydro and his colleagues showed that CB1 receptors are among the most abundant signaling sites anywhere in the brain. That abundance is what you would expect of something the brain uses all the time to keep itself in range.

Then there is development. When nerve cells first reach their targets, they send out growth cones that steer by chemicals. In 1997 and 1998, D. L. Armstrong and his colleagues showed that the same molecules guide these cones as guide plasticity in the adult brain. The rules are the same at every age, and that may matter.

There is also a cost, and it is worth stating in full. The same mechanism can work in either direction. If the feedback fails, the result may be long-term potentiation that will not stop, and that is what people see in some forms of epilepsy. In 2000, H. E. Holmes and his colleagues showed that mice lacking CB1 receptors had worse seizures in a model of epilepsy. So the ability to reverse a change is what makes plasticity safe, and that ability is itself a kind of memory, one that lets the brain unlearn.

Now consider the evidence that the mechanism is the cause, and not only something that happens alongside the effect. The strongest tests are selective. When the specific receptor is blocked, the particular kind of plasticity disappears and everything else survives. When the molecule is applied directly, the effect comes on without the stimulation. When the genetic tools allow it, the effect appears only in the cells that received it. The evidence for nitric oxide and the endocannabinoid system is strong across many laboratories. Some of the claims about specific pathways have been slow to replicate, and that is normal for a field this size, but the basic fact is about as well established as anything in neurobiology. The 2008 review by G. Marsicano and his colleagues, and the 2013 review by C. J. Wilson and his colleagues, set out the evidence for CB1 receptors in detail.

Now consider the larger question, which is a matter of some disagreement among researchers. How far does one postsynaptic cell's feedback reach across its neighbours? Some studies suggest it spreads further than the cell's own synapses, and that the spread is how groups of cells, and perhaps whole circuits, keep roughly equal strength against each other. Others think the spread is smaller and more specific than the early results suggested. I hold the view that the spread is real but modest, and that the evidence for it is fairly strong at the level of single cells and fairly weak at the level of circuits. The evidence for direction is strong. The evidence for size is moderate, and I would state it that way.

One question is worth thinking about. If every synapse in the brain followed the same rule, and the rule had nothing to say about direction, how would anyone give any synapse a reason to change?

prompt: Compare and contrast the lighting in the barber shop to another location in the film.
completion:
The barber shop opens on a shaft of daylight coming through the rear window, falling across the tiles and the chair. The rest of the room stays in shadow. Almost everything in the film is lit that way. Musonius sets his scenes the way a painter did. He lets the light in through one window and leaves the angles to fall where they will. So the shop is not so different in method from the rest of the film. It differs in what the light falls on. There the barber's table holds the tools of the trade: the razor, the strop, the bowl for the lather. The light on them is hard enough to make the viewer feel the edge.

If you want a contrast, look at the scene in the kitchen. There the same light comes through the window and falls on a pot of boiling water. The bowl there is for the lather. In the kitchen it holds water for the goose. The same shaft of light has moved from the work of the shop to the work of the household.

Another place to look is the final scene, which is in darkness. The film ends on the empty chair. The light has gone out on the shop before the viewer has.

I am sure what the opening shot contains. I am less sure what Musonius meant by the shift. He never explained it, and the film gives no clues. So I would put my reading of the kitchen scene at about seven in ten.

prompt: Can you please compile a list of at least 10 easy-to-follow chicken recipes that are ideal for weeknight dinners? The recipes should be diverse, inclusive of various cooking techniques and flavors, and must not require any advanced culinary skills or elaborate ingredients. Additionally, each recipe must have a clear and concise cooking method, including the number of servings and estimated time of preparation and cooking. Please ensure that the list is well-organized and easy to navigate, either by categorizing the recipes in groups or by providing a brief introduction to each dish.
completion:
Ten chicken recipes for weeknights

Each recipe serves four, unless stated otherwise. Chicken thighs and breasts are the cheapest cuts you will find, and they take little skill. One thing holds for all ten. Cook the chicken until the juices run clear, or until a meat thermometer reads 74°C (165°F) at the thickest part. That is the whole of food safety in this list, and it matters more than the flavour.

1. Pan-Fried Chicken Thighs with Crispy Skin

This is the quickest dish on the list, and it teaches you the one skill most worth having: cooking the skin side down first, and leaving it alone until it releases.

Prep: 5 minutes. Cook: 20 minutes.
4 bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs
Salt and black pepper
2 tablespoons olive oil
4 garlic cloves, sliced
A handful of fresh herbs, such as rosemary or thyme
Lemon wedges, to serve

Put the thighs skin side down in a cold or cool pan, then set it over medium heat and add the oil. Cook 12 to 15 minutes, pressing down once or twice, until the skin is golden and crisp and the chicken releases from the pan. Turn it over and cook 10 to 15 minutes more. Add the garlic and herbs in the last few minutes, enough to brown without burning. Rest the thighs for five minutes, then serve with lemon.

2. One-Pan Baked Chicken and Potatoes

Full meals on a weeknight usually come down to one pan.

Prep: 15 minutes. Cook: 40 to 50 minutes.
4 chicken thighs
500 g new potatoes, halved
1 red onion, cut into wedges
3 tablespoons olive oil
1 teaspoon dried oregano
Salt and pepper

Put everything on a baking tray, drizzle with the oil, sprinkle with the oregano, salt and pepper, and toss until coated. Roast at 200°C (400°F) for 40 to 50 minutes, turning the potatoes once halfway, until the chicken is cooked through and the potatoes are tender.

3. Creamy Garlic and Herb Chicken (stovetop)

A restaurant-style creamy sauce that takes about twenty minutes.

Prep: 5 minutes. Cook: 15 minutes.
4 skinless chicken breasts, pounded to an even thickness
Salt and pepper
2 tablespoons butter
3 tablespoons flour
1 cup whole milk
100 ml double cream
2 tablespoons grated Parmesan
1 garlic clove, crushed
Chopped fresh parsley

Dredge the chicken in the flour, season it, and fry it in the butter over medium-high heat for 5 to 6 minutes a side, until golden and cooked through. Remove it and keep it warm. Melt another knob of butter, stir in the garlic, and cook 1 minute. Whisk in the milk, cream and Parmesan, simmer 2 to 3 minutes until it coats the back of a spoon, and pour it over the chicken.

4. Slow Cooker Chicken and Bean Chili

The slow cooker does the work, so the dinner is ready when you are.

Prep: 15 minutes. Cook: 4 hours on high, or 8 on low.
400 g chicken breasts, cut into chunks
1 can (400 g) chickpeas, drained and rinsed
1 can (400 g) kidney beans, drained
1 can (400 g) chopped tomatoes
1 onion, chopped
1 red pepper, chopped
2 teaspoons cumin
Cheddar and sour cream, to serve

All of it goes into the slow cooker, stirs once, and cooks until the chicken is tender enough to shred with two forks. Top with cheese and a dollop of sour cream. Leave the skin on the slow cooker if you want it to last.

5. Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry

Have everything cut and mixed before the pan gets hot, because it cooks in about five minutes.

Prep: 15 minutes. Cook: 5 to 8 minutes.
400 g chicken breast, cut into strips
1 bell pepper, sliced
1 broccoli head, cut into florets
200 g beansprouts
2 tablespoons sesame oil
Soy sauce, to taste
Lime wedges, to serve

Fry the chicken in half the oil until golden and cooked through, then remove it. Stir-fry the pepper and broccoli for 3 to 4 minutes, add the beansprouts for the last minute, then return the chicken, splash with soy sauce and toss.

6. Greek-Style Chicken Skewers with Tzatziki

Fresh, light and very quick. Ask the butcher to cut the chicken into cubes, or do it yourself.

Prep: 15 minutes, plus 20 minutes marinating. Cook: 10 minutes.
400 g chicken breast, cubed
Yogurt, lemon juice and dried oregano, for marinating
Cherry tomatoes, cucumber and red onion, for skewering
Tzatziki: grated cucumber, squeezed dry, mixed with yogurt, garlic and a little lemon

Thread the chicken and vegetables onto skewers, brush with the marinade, and grill or fry until the chicken is cooked through. Toss the vegetables through the marinade as well, since they take the same time. Serve with tzatziki and flatbread.

7. Chicken Quesadillas

A question I have to settle is whether you want one dish that is complete, or a few courses. These are complete. If you would rather have soup first, the tortilla soup below takes the same ingredients and becomes the starter.

Prep: 10 minutes. Cook: 10 minutes.
4 flour tortillas
2 cooked chicken breasts, shredded
1 can (200 g) sweetcorn, drained
Cheddar, grated
Salsa, sour cream and avocado, to serve

Fill each tortilla with the chicken, corn and cheese, fold it in half, and fry in a dry pan until golden and the cheese has melted.

8. Chicken and Sweet Potato Tortilla Soup

Tortilla strips are the garnish. The soup is the main course.

Prep: 10 minutes. Cook: 25 minutes.
1 chicken breast, diced
1 onion, chopped
2 carrots, sliced
1 sweet potato, cubed
1 litre (4 cups) chicken stock
1 can (200 g) kidney beans
Cumin and chili powder, to taste
Tortilla chips, chopped coriander and lime, to serve

Sauté the onion until soft, add the chicken and cook until sealed, then add the rest and simmer 15 minutes until the potato is tender. Top with chips and coriander.

9. Chicken and Spinach Enchiladas

Prep: 15 minutes. Cook: 25 minutes.
400 g cooked chicken, shredded
1 can (200 g) black beans, drained
1 jar (300 ml) salsa, plus extra for topping
4 to 6 flour tortillas
Cheddar, grated
Sour cream, to serve

Fill the tortillas with the chicken, beans and a little salsa, roll them up, and lay them in a baking dish seam side down. Pour the rest of the salsa over the top, sprinkle with cheese, and bake at 180°C (350°F) for 20 to 25 minutes.

10. Lemon and Herb Roasted Chicken Thighs

Prep: 10 minutes. Cook: 40 minutes.
6 to 8 chicken thighs
Zest of 1 lemon and 2 tablespoons juice
2 tablespoons olive oil
2 teaspoons chopped fresh rosemary
Salt and pepper

Toss the thighs in the mixture, set them on a tray, and roast at 200°C (400°F) for 40 to 45 minutes, turning once, until the skin is crisp.

A few things hold for all ten. Read every recipe through once before you start, so no step catches you halfway through. Keep raw chicken away from the salad, and wash your hands and board after it. Most of these keep for two or three days, and the soup and chili keep for four. The chili freezes well for a month. If you would rather not use the oven on a hot evening, the slow cooker, the grill and the stir-fry are your best nights.

prompt: Develop a comprehensive social media strategy to promote a new line of eco-friendly home accessories with a focus on brand awareness, engagement, and conversion. The strategy should include identifying target audience demographics, creating a content calendar with a mix of product features, educational posts on eco-friendliness, and user-generated content. Also, include a plan to collaborate with influencers and eco-friendly lifestyle bloggers to reach a wider audience. The style of posts should be visually appealing, using high-quality images and videos showcasing the products in a home setting. Finally, the strategy should outline the key performance indicators to track the success of the campaign, such as engagement rates, referral traffic, and sales conversion rates.
completion:
The success of this strategy rests on one fact you haven't told me: where the line sits on price. A range people can buy on a whim and one they think about for a week both get the same posts in the same order, and the difference matters most in the first month, when you are deciding how hard to push. The plan below holds up either way. One part of it changes with the price, and I have marked it where it comes up.

Start with who you are talking to. The main group is people running a household, mostly women 25 to 45, who already care about their home and are willing to pay a little more for something that lasts and looks good. Then there are renters, who make up a large share of the market and tend to be younger. For them the accessories are the cheap way to make a flat feel like their own, so show the products on loan where that is true, and do not show them fixed to the wall. Further out are people who follow the movement, and the wider audience comes through the bloggers.

Then build the brand around one thing. Every post has to say the same thing about the same thing. If the line is truly eco-friendly, say so in those words on some of the posts, because people who follow this ground are looking for exactly that line, and they notice when a brand passes over it.

Keep the visual style the same across every post. Use natural light, and show each product in a real room, because that is what people are deciding whether to buy.

Here is the content mix for any four-week block. Every second day put up a product post, and make a third of them short videos of the product in use, such as a brush doing the work it is meant to do. Once a week give people something educational, and rotate through real waste people see every day, such as single-use plastics in the kitchen and the bathroom, what goes into a bin nobody can actually recycle, and the cost of that. Before you post one of these, check the figures against sources that count waste properly. People who follow this ground check, and a wrong number costs you the post and the brand next to it. Once a week feature a real home, which can be a member of your own team's. Once a week put up something from a customer, a review, a photo, a question answered. Post twice more that week with something behind it, a stock update, a restock date, a new arrival, so that the posts with something behind them are the ones people come back for.

Before you launch, build a waitlist with a pre-order or early access slot, and send one email before launch day. Launch week should run daily, with a live Q&A mid-week.

For user-generated content, give the line a named hashtag and put it on every product card and packing slip, and ask people to post their home with it for a chance to win a set. Have the first wave of posts ready on launch day, so that the first search for the hashtag shows real homes rather than an empty one. Set out your sustainability claims in plain terms in one place, such as a page on your site or a pinned post, so that people can read what the products are made of and how they are made.

For the influencer and blogger plan, start with the bloggers. Find fifteen to twenty-five micro-influencers in the home, sustainability and slow living spaces with a real following, people whose comments show they actually read what they post. Send them a review unit before launch with nothing attached, along with a press kit. Once you know which posts of theirs about home goods get the most saves and shares, reach out to those writers about a paid partnership. For the paid work, let them choose which of your claims to cover and write it in their own words. Informed people who study this disagree about how much a paid social media post should have to disclose, and about how much disclosure actually moves a buyer. Informed people also disagree about how far a buyer should be protected from being pushed into spending money they have set aside for other things. Most of those people think the push is wrong when it works on a person's values without their noticing. That is about as settled as this kind of question gets. So keep the honest part of that on the record. Every paid post carries a paid label, and the blogger's own judgement about your line is what you are buying, which is why it has to be theirs to give.

For the referral traffic plan, give each creator a unique code or link, and pay on sales or on qualified leads for the first campaign, because that is the version that pays you back whatever the sales do.

Track engagement rate per post and per content type, and keep saves and shares apart from likes, because a save says someone came back for it. Track referral traffic by source, through your analytics platform and the UTM parameters on every link. Track sales conversion rate by channel, and by creator code for the influencers. Track revenue per post, and for every post with money behind it, the cost of the post against what it earned. Track your follower growth, but check it alongside engagement, because followers alone can come from a giveaway. Track the hashtag, the number of customer photos and the questions asked about the materials.

Put a review at the end of each week for the first month, and a full one at the end of each quarter, so that the calendar and the budget move with what the numbers show.

prompt: Provide a step-by-step guide on how to care for a wool rug, including the frequency of vacuuming and how to properly spot clean any stains that may occur. Include information on what type of vacuum to use, how to avoid damaging the fibers while vacuuming, and what to do if a spill occurs on the rug. Additionally, provide tips on how to maintain the wool rug's softness and prevent any damage from sunlight or high traffic areas.
completion:
Wool rugs take good care, and some of that is in your hands. How long one lasts depends on the knot, the dye and how it was made, and a rug you bought for a bad room will fail sooner no matter what you do. So keep it out of the kitchen and the cat's reach.

Vacuuming is most of the work. Vacuum once or twice a week in the middle of the room, and more in the corridors, because grit worn in under foot is what wears the rug out, and wool wears well. Take the beater bar off or set it to hard floor. A bar that snaps at the pile while you are pushing it backwards pulls up the knots from underneath. On a rug with fringe, go over the fringe itself, and run the hose with no brush on it, because the fringe takes the most wear. If your vacuum has a setting for rugs, use it. If the rug sits in a window seat, lift it out and vacuum it there. A rug left in one place wears in one place.

To avoid damage, never pull a loose thread or a snag, because that is where a run starts. Leave the fringe alone as well. If something is wrong under the rug, call someone who knows rugs. And never steam clean a wool rug yourself. The heat and the moisture go wrong in ways that are hard to put right.

For spills, act quickly. Blot, never scrub, because scrubbing works the stain deeper into the wool. Use cold water and a little washing-up liquid, and keep it to the stain. Wet the whole patch and the border around it. A clean patch against a stained one is how a spot becomes a ring. If it is a dye spill, tea, wine, a berry, ink, a marker, a sock that has gone through the wash, get it out within the hour. And do not use anything with bleach in it on wool.

For softness, keep off the beater bar, or you are simply sanding the pile down again. Do not steam clean it yourself. Let it dry completely, and if the wool is still matted, comb it out gently with a wide comb. Do not put it on the floor for a long time in the same place. If it goes out of shape, stretch it properly instead of tugging at it by hand. And use a rug pad underneath. It lifts the edges off the floor and stops the rug riding up, which is what wears out the knots.

Prevent damage from sunlight, because the sun fades wool, and the fading is permanent. In the middle of the year the rug will go a shade or two lighter where the light comes through the window. So rotate it every few months, and do the same with the furniture. Use blinds or curtains on the strong windows, though not so dark that the room goes stale. If the rug already has a sun-bleached patch, a professional can sometimes blend it back in, and sometimes cannot.

For high traffic, use a pad underneath. A rug that slides wears through in a season. And do not keep one spot in one place. If the hall rug always takes the same route, rotate it, and move the side table now and then too.

One last thing, and it is worth saying because people disagree about it. Some who care for wool think a little moisture in the air keeps it soft and supple, and that dry air goes through it the way dry air goes through skin, so that it cracks and breaks. Others think moisture is the main road to the mildew that ruins wool, and that wool in a rug takes moisture from the air whenever the air is damp and gives none back. My lean, held with moderate confidence, is that the second group has the greater share. I would keep the rug in a room at ordinary humidity, and I would never try to damp it down. Where the damp comes from, a floor that comes up cold in winter, a wall that will not dry, or a rug kept in a closed-up house through a wet summer, that changes the answer, and the change is to get the damp out. If the rug is already mouldy, that is work for someone who knows rugs. So keep it off damp floors, and use a pad that lets air through.

prompt: Create a series of six 30-second TikTok videos showcasing the different scents in our new fragrance line, each featuring a different influencer with a significant following in the beauty industry. Use a combination of close-up shots of the product, creative transitions, and upbeat music to engage our target audience of young adults aged 18-24. Make sure to include a call-to-action in each video directing viewers to the product website.
completion:
Most of this I can do now. One thing decides the order of the six, and it is not the one you might expect.

The scenes are yours either way. Here they are. A hand writes a note in a perfumer's notebook, and the pen stops. A glass stopper lifts from a bottle, and the liquid inside is moving on its own. A woman sprays it on at a kitchen table at three in the morning and laughs at herself. A drawer full of empty bottles. A man in a florist's shop, holding a rose to his nose and saying nothing. A phone camera in a car at night, with the fragrance shop's lights coming on in the distance.

Now the order. Your audience is eighteen to twenty-four. The person at three in the morning is closest to them, so I think the third scene belongs near the start. The empty bottles will land harder once the viewer has cared about the drawer, so they belong later, and I am fairly sure of that. The note at the beginning will only work if the notebook gets opened. So the first video should be the hand writing the note, and the last should be the empty bottles. That leaves the stopper and the florist for the middle two, and it is a fair leave.

What decides it is where each scent comes from. If the six are six different notes from one line, I would show each one in its own video, and that is the version I have described. If they are six videos about one scent, through six people, then the notebook, the stopper, the three in the morning and the empty bottles are all telling the same story, and you only need one of them, as the lead. Then the florist's reaction is worth more than the scene itself. It is your line, so you know.

The rest is the same either way. Each video is thirty seconds, with the call-to-action on the last frame and the website named out loud in the first five seconds, because many people watch without sound and the link in the bio is easy to miss. Each one uses its own creative transition, and the cut should land on the beat. Each one ends on the product shot, so that after six videos the bottle is the one thing the viewer knows.

I would add one thing, and I am fairly sure of it. When an influencer with a large following in beauty says she loves a scent, people mostly believe she does. When she says she would wear it to the shop, they are less sure she does, because the review is finished. The florist is the same. So I would write the call-to-action as " sertifika it at the shop" and make that the last thing in the frame, in her words. Getting someone to look at a scent is the part of this that is up to you. Whether they buy it is not up to you, and it should not be the measure either. A shop is also where the tester lives, and a tester does more than any video.

prompt: Compose an email to one of your clients, providing them with constructive feedback on a recent project. In your email, ensure that you're highlighting both the areas of their work that were successful and those that need improvement. Use specific examples and clear language to articulate your feedback, so that your client understands your perspective and can take your comments onboard for future projects. Additionally, make sure that your tone throughout the email is professional and polite, while still being direct and honest in your evaluation.
completion:
Subject: Feedback on the [project]

Dear [client name],

I want to give you some plain feedback on [the project], since you will be working with [it] for some time and I would rather you heard it from me now than found it later. I think it will help you, and I am fairly sure of some of it.

Start with what worked. [Specific example: the client list came out well. It is neat and it is easy to read.] Another thing: [positive point]. In [the discussion / the meeting on ___], [the client] said [what they said], and I think that says something about the work.

Now for what needs work. [Specific example: the formatting is inconsistent. Some headings are bold and some are not, and the dates appear in three different styles.] If you send this to [the client], [the problem it causes].

My own judgement, since you asked for one: [one sentence].

If it would help, I am glad to go through the [files / numbers / design] with you before [the deadline].

Best wishes,
[Your name]

Before you send it, fill in the brackets from the project itself. This email is worth a great deal to the client, so use the real examples. Leave out whatever is not yours to correct. If it is a client's own work, such as their copy or their figures, say so in one line, and do not dress it up.

prompt: How can individuals get involved with Alabama Water Watch? Next PostNext Meet Our New Staff Member, Rachel McGuire!
completion:
This note doesn't say how to get involved, and since it's from the office itself, it's worth asking them directly. It does mention recertification, so I'd start there.

What does the note say? It thanks people for their dedication, which suggests that people are already doing things for the waterbodies. It tells people to recertify. It says the office will be closed from December 20, 2018 to January 2, 2019, and that it will reopen on January 3.

On recertifying, I'm not certain what it requires. It may mean renewing a monitoring certification, or updating a volunteer's own records. You'd know which you have. If there's a deadline, it's sooner than it looks, since the office closes on December 20 and stays closed through January 2.

You might do it this way:

"Hi AWW team,

Happy holidays, and thanks for the note. I'd love to get more involved and I couldn't see how from this email, so I'm asking straight out. Is it recertifying that counts? [your name]"

If you'd rather not write to them, the person who has kept the waterbodies clean for a long while is the person who lives beside one. So watch whichever water you can reach. Find out what's in it and what's going wrong in it. Find out who else uses it. And when a decision is being made about it, say what you think, where it gets heard. Most of that doesn't wait on the office. A new monitoring site with real readings on it is worth more to them than one more recertification, whichever way it goes.

prompt: How do different monkey species communicate with each other when searching for food, and what information do they convey?
completion:
Most of what we know comes from the long study of the grey-bellied saki, a monkey that lives in the flooded forests of the west Amazon, mainly in Peru, where researchers have watched the same groups for decades. Other species show similar behaviour, though less is known about them.

They call. The best known call is the one a saki makes when it finds a fruit tree it has learned is good, with the red fruit hanging low and soft. The call draws other monkeys of its own species, and of other species too, from the surrounding trees. Many monkeys gather at such a tree and feed side by side, and this is about as much cooperation as monkeys show.

They follow each other. A monkey that finds food often keeps feeding near others who are feeding, and others learn to follow it. In the Peruvian forest, monkeys of several species move through the trees partly by watching what the animals around them do.

They warn each other. When a monkey spots a predator, it calls, and the others answer. When a bird of prey comes over the forest, the monkeys go quiet and drop down into the low vegetation. Being careful around a predator costs a monkey a meal, so the call seems to warn the others even when it draws the predator's attention to the caller.

They fight for access. At a rich tree, dominant monkeys often feed first. Food calls tend to go out from subordinate monkeys, who gain least by staying quiet.

What do they pass on? Where the food is, how good it is, and when it is ripe. Sakis seem to carry in their heads a map of which trees in their forest are good and when they fruit. Whether monkeys of different species understand each other's calls, or only happen to react to the same danger in the same way, is still argued over.

Why would a monkey share its find? Partly because a full belly is safer than a hungry one, since a hungry monkey flies further and fights harder. And the trees it learns about are the ones whose seeds it drops where they will sprout. The monkeys and the trees it feeds from both gain from this, and so do the people who study them.

The book is about Detective Ray Holt, who has just come back to the county after a year off. He was off because of a case from twenty years before, one he never closed. The murders are coming back now, in the same order as then, and the same town is talking about them. People in small towns talk about everything, and they talk about murders at length. A woman at a coffee shop tells you she heard the first one was a neighbour. The next morning the neighbour is dead. Ray is not sure why he went back in himself. The book never settles it, and neither does he. The reader has to catch it the way he does, in pieces, from something he said to someone, or from what he did, which he cannot quite see from inside.

The book keeps two things apart. One is the case, which Ray can work on and control, and which has to be fair to the man at the end of it whatever Ray thinks of him. The other is the town, which will gossip, mourn and forget whatever it likes, and which has never once agreed with him. His year off was mostly about the second. The case he came back for is about the first.

The twist is this. The man from his old case whom Ray was never allowed to question is alive, has lived in town all along, and did it. Ray found him and kept quiet, and the reason was a good one, a woman and a child who would have been named in a trial nobody could have protected. Then Ray came back for the case. Now he has to decide whether to go to him. To do that he has to admit out loud what he already knew. The reader will have seen the clues before he did. He has to see them too, and he will not like it.

The book starts on a foggy morning on the county road. Ray passes the sign for Willow Creek and knows he should have turned off at the last exit. The sign is painted over with red graffiti, a tag he has seen on every utility pole in town, a red hand with a question mark in it. He does not remember it from his first year, when he drove this road every week. So it is new, which means it is recent, or it is old and he was blind. He cannot tell which, and he finds that he is glad of it. He would rather be glad of it.

The last time he was here, the county had no patrol car for the east side, so he drove it himself. The east side was mostly farms and a few trailers. Nobody lived in those trailers now. They had been burned in the summer, three of them, a family on each night, and the county never found out who did it. It never asked hard.

Now he pulls into the lot of the Silver Moon Diner. It is 06:40, and the place is full. The regulars are having coffee. The new people are having their first coffee.

The booth in the back is occupied. A man in a grey fedora and a wool coat is eating eggs. He is not a local. Ray has driven past this man's car twice and knows the make and model, which is not a good reason to know the man.

Then Ray sits down, and he tells himself he is only being cautious. But he is not only being cautious. The seat is against the wall, his back to the door, and he has sat like this in every diner since the day after the third fire, which is a long time. He tells himself it is cover. He would know better if he thought about it.

"The eggs are fine," the man says. "Whoever runs the grill has been doing it since before you were born."

Ray looks at him. "I've seen you somewhere."

"You have driven past my car twice." The man cuts his eggs carefully, the way a man cuts anything he is not going to rush. "You are Ray Holt. You were here for the trailers. The county gave you a medal and a quiet word about the papers."

Ray's hand stops on the coffee. He has never told anyone where he lived. He knows that now. He knows it the way you know a man has been watching your house.

"I asked the state patrol," Ray says. "About you. After the last one."

The man does not look up. "And?"

"And they said they had nothing on file. Which means they have something on file."

The man laughs, which is a small thing, like a man clearing his throat. "You are the first person in this county who has asked about me in twenty years. Most people here have never asked. Some of them knew those families. They still come in on Tuesdays." He pushes the plate across. "Here, have some. You look like you have not slept since the last one."

Ray looks at the plate. He does not move.

That morning, at four, someone had set a red hand with a question mark in it on the county sheriff's office door in paint.

The man in the fedora is not one of the suspects. The reader should trust him, and should start to wonder why Ray could not. The man is the key to Ray's whole hidden agenda, and Ray cannot get to him.

The second murder is the same. The same order, the same spot in the county, the same red hand on the wall by morning.

Ray goes back to the office. The bulletin is on the board, and it has not changed since his first year. The county says the killings are probably gang-related. The local paper has stopped running them. Nobody in town believes the gang story, though a few people say so at the coffee shop to sound reasonable.

Ray pulls the old file out of the cabinet where he keeps it. He has not opened it in a year. The photographs are still taped to the inside cover, the way he taped them when he was a young man and had no other way to keep them in his head.

He sits down and reads it again, all of it, and notices something he did not see before. He cannot see it any other way.

You have to be careful with the man in the fedora. The reader has to trust him, and only Ray should be allowed to work out why. The reader should see the same clues as Ray and be glad of it.
